The T1 script supplies distance explicitly, so the frame’s default cluster distance is overridden (sun_dist_bar_grids.py:18–20, grid4_common.py:40–49).

docs.title: Direct answers
docs.text:
(a) T1 is not a projection-only test. make_spray uses one frame both to convert the cluster’s observed state into the model-frame initial condition and to convert the resulting debris back to observables (grid4_common.py:40–50). Thus the swap changes the inferred Galactocentric orbit and the projection. The host setup is unchanged for these runs, but the cluster’s initial state in that host is not (grid4_common.py:46–49; restricted.py:68–84).

For a fixed Galactocentric trajectory at 4 kpc, a 20 km/s transverse observer-velocity shift corresponds to about 1.05 mas/yr, so projection alone is large enough in scale to matter. But T1 does not hold that trajectory fixed: its frame change also alters the initial condition. The packet reports that at \(d=5.6\) kpc the W–R16 gap changes from −782 to −93 in the two frames, with W’s gain concentrated in the outer segment and losses near the cluster; those figures are reported results, not independently recomputed here (packet:2025–2034). They do not isolate reflex from orbit changes.

(b) The proposed decomposition is the right idea, but implement it as two independent frame choices. Cross initial-condition frame with projection frame: Baumgardt IC/Baumgardt projection, Baumgardt IC/Ibata projection, Ibata IC/Baumgardt projection, Ibata IC/Ibata projection. Run at a fixed distance first; then repeat at the alternative distance if needed. The current API cannot express this: make_spray has only one frame argument (grid4_common.py:40–50). Save the model-frame particle states and reproject those same trajectories under both projection frames; this avoids duplicate integrations for the projection-only comparison.

A host \(v_c(R_0)\) sweep is a separate experiment, not a prerequisite for this decomposition. The packet reports the host at 228.8 km/s, while the Ibata frame’s stated solar velocity is constructed using 220 km/s plus 12.24 km/s peculiar motion (packet:2020–2025, frames.py:7–8, 16–18). That mismatch matters when interpreting a physically self-consistent solar-motion model. Test it separately by varying host normalization and solar motion together under a stated relation, while keeping the observed heliocentric cluster data fixed.

(c) Cost-aware order:

  1. Run the IC × projection factorial at one distance, preferably 5.6 kpc, then at 5.43 kpc if the result depends on IC frame. Decision rule: if the score gain follows projection frame with either IC, reflex/projection dominates; if it follows IC with either projection, orbit changes dominate; if there is a large interaction, the effects are coupled.
  2. Separate the remaining frame ingredients with one-at-a-time controls: \(V_{\odot,y}\), \(R_0\), and \(z_\odot\). Then run the host-\(v_c\)/solar-motion-consistency sweep. Decision rule: call the 15–20 km/s shift an orbit/potential effect only if it survives the projection-only control and moves coherently with the host or initial-condition change.
  3. Extend the bar grid at its current boundaries: test \(\Omega_b<34\) at 16° and amplitude \(>1.4\) at 28°/size 1.3, while retaining common seeds and scoring. Both optima are reported at explored edges, so the current grid cannot establish either as an optimum (packet:2036–2046). Decision rule: require an interior preference and a gain larger than the reported roughly ±36 lnL spray noise (packet:2046–2048).
  4. Try LMC forcing after these controls. It adds a potential/reflex change and therefore cannot cleanly explain the shift until the simpler frame and host effects are separated.

(d) Code audit: The frame round trip is internally paired: to_model and observables use matching sign flips for model \(x\) and \(v_x\) (frames.py:31–39, 48–56). The relevant gap is test coverage: I found no direct test of these stream-frame transforms or their round trip; the existing frame test covers a different progenitor-orbit module (test_progenitor_orbits.py:8–22). score_conditional has tests for background-only cases, density cancellation, bin duplication, and degraded kinematics (test_score_conditional.py:24–65), but the supplied tests do not establish its behavior for invalid covariance matrices, empty data, or measured radial velocities.

One data-safety issue in the T1 runner: it rewrites the accumulated JSON result file directly after each run, without an atomic replace; interruption during the write can leave a damaged checkpoint (sun_dist_bar_grids.py:25–26, 41–42). The per-run NPZ is written first, which provides some recovery, but the runner reads the JSON before resuming (sun_dist_bar_grids.py:33–38).

docs.title: What I verified and what I assumed
docs.text:
I verified the frame definitions, the shared IC/projection frame parameter, the host construction path, the score implementation and its tests, and the result-writing order by reading the cited code. The reported likelihoods, segment shifts, host circular speed, and spray-noise estimate come from the packet; I did not independently rerun the simulations or verify those outputs (packet:2019–2048).

I assume the score and the reported results are comparable across frames, the saved/recomputed spray trajectories use identical physical inputs and seeds, and the packet’s approximate reflex estimate refers to a transverse velocity difference at about 4 kpc.

docs.title: Strongest argument against this answer
docs.text: The reported outer-stream improvement is large and has the sign expected from a changed solar reflex, while the host is held fixed. That makes projection a plausible major contributor. But because each T1 run also changes the cluster’s inferred initial condition—and changes \(R_0\) and \(z_\odot\)—the table cannot show that projection is the dominant cause.

docs.title: What I would check to be sure
docs.text:
• Implement and inspect the crossed IC/projection comparison, including the proposed distances.
  • Verify the reported lnL and segment values from the saved NPZ files and result table.
  • Add direct transform round-trip tests for both frames, and score tests with finite radial velocities and malformed covariances.
  • Check that the JSON checkpoint survives interruption and can resume from the saved NPZ files.

docs.title: Codex code review 2026 10 10
docs.text: The code does not establish a definite handedness, arm-sign, or observable-conversion bug. It does expose a more immediate issue for interpreting the results: the grid score is designed to ignore stream density along the tail, while it excludes model particles older than 700 Myr. That makes the 700 Myr cut a relevant scoring sensitivity, but the score cannot by itself explain the visible thinning as a count mismatch. (score.py:233, score.py:250)

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• No clear reflection error in the observable round trip. to_model flips the Astropy x position and velocity; observables flips them back before transforming to ICRS. That is internally consistent in the code. (frames.py:31, frames.py:48)

  • No obvious sign inversion in the release basis. rj_vj_R builds its second axis as L × r, and release_ic offsets the arm=+1 particle to positive radial x with a positive tangential velocity offset for a positive-Lz orbit. That is consistent with the stated outer/trailing convention, but the comments and equations do not verify the result dynamically. (spray.py:25, spray.py:31, spray.py:49, spray.py:57)

  • The trailing-arm selection is not independently validated by the scoring path. The grid keeps arm == 1, while score_conditional separately drops particles with chi <= 0. If those labels disagree, the selected model stream is silently reduced or altered. (grid4.py:36, score.py:250)

Minimal test: on representative and circular synthetic orbits, report the fraction of each arm with chi > 0 and the sign of its psi. Check that arm +1 is consistently the trailing branch over the release window before scoring.

  • The 700 Myr age cut can affect angle ranking. Grid sprays release over 1000 Myr, but scoring retains only particles with age < 700; the model’s effective age range can also depend on which chi bins meet nmin=20. (grid4.py:27, score.py:250, score.py:253)

Minimal test: rescore the existing 1000 Myr sprays with age limits 500, 700, and 1000 Myr; report the angle ranking and per-star likelihood changes by phi1. This is cheaper and more informative than first generating longer sprays.

  • The conditional score cannot test the observed thinning as a count discrepancy. It forms a density in observables conditional on along-stream position by dividing by the along-stream marginal. Where model support is weak, the background mixture takes over. Thus this score can compare track and kinematic agreement, but it is not evidence that the model predicts the observed number of stars along the tail. (score.py:233, score.py:240, score.py:273)

Minimal test: compare angle rankings from the current conditional score with an explicitly defined count or coverage diagnostic, while accounting for catalogue completeness and selection. Do not treat raw particle counts as observed counts without that model.

  • Data loading leaves a numerical-integrity check outstanding. The cuts select stream 54 by sky position, but do not filter nonfinite PMs, PM errors, or correlations. Those values feed directly into the likelihood covariance calculation. (spray_bar_grid2.py:27, spray_bar_grid2.py:28, spray_bar_grid2.py:30, score.py:259)

Minimal test: assert all selected PMs, errors, and correlations are finite, all uncertainties are positive, and every covariance determinant is positive. The source-ID equality assertion checks row alignment, not those conditions. (spray_bar_grid2.py:26)

docs.title: Revised experiment order
docs.text:
1. Run the end-to-end checks still outstanding: to_model/observables round trip; synthetic circular-orbit release basis; arm versus chi sign; and catalogue finite-value/covariance checks. The packet says the derivative, bar-angle-time, and centre-orbit checks already passed, so repeating those is lower priority.
  2. Rescore cached sprays across age limits and inspect per-star contributions by phi1. The current code supports this without another integration. (grid4.py:31, score.py:250)
  3. Compare segment and observable residuals, then run mock recovery to test whether the angle preference is calibrated under the score. The grid holds the cluster PMs fixed while varying bar parameters and distance, so its angle maximum is conditional on that fixed state. (grid4.py:20, grid4.py:35)
  4. Use the supplied 200k-tracer run as evidence against the spray release prescription being the sole cause of the miss, as the packet reports the same miss at 20 degrees. Test a different bar angle or centre state before repeating that comparison at 20 degrees.
  5. Extend the release window beyond 1000 Myr only if existing sprays show that older particles would contribute; first establish the effect of the existing 700 Myr scoring cut.

docs.title: Verified, assumed, and remaining checks
docs.text:
Verified by reading the code: the x reflection is applied symmetrically in the conversion functions; the release basis uses L × r; the grid selects arm +1; the score filters on chi > 0 and age < age_max; the conditional score divides by its along-stream marginal; and the data loader’s cuts do not include explicit finite-PM/covariance validation. (frames.py:31, spray.py:31, grid4.py:36, score.py:250, score.py:273, spray_bar_grid2.py:28)

Assumptions: I accept the packet’s reported astrometric residuals, catalogue size, 200k-tracer miss, and previous audit results as inputs; I did not reproduce those runs. I also assume the external Hunter potential assets use the intended model-frame orientation.

Strongest argument against this assessment: the most consequential remaining defect could be in the external potential’s rotation convention or in its mapping to the reflected model frame. The source documents the intended angle convention, but source inspection alone cannot prove that the external potential rotates in that sense. (restricted.py:43, restricted.py:51)

To be sure: run the four end-to-end/data checks above; inspect likelihood contributions by age and phi1; and verify the external potential’s rotation direction against an independently transformed positive-longitude near end. The supplied test coverage includes focused score and spin tests, but the visible test references do not cover the release-basis, arm/chi, or end-to-end frame checks proposed here. (test_score_conditional.py:24, test_spray_spin.py:14)

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
The premise is broadly correct for score_chi_kde: it makes a 4D KDE in \((l,b,\mu_{\alpha*},\mu_\delta)\) within each \(\chi\) bin, then averages the bin densities with equal weights. The sky coordinates are part of each KDE, so the likelihood retains the model’s density along the stream. The module header describes a different scorer, score(), and is stale for score_chi_kde. score.py:1–11, score.py:151–160

Use the proposed ratio of the joint mixture to its along-coordinate marginal, with an explicit conditional background. If \(f_k(u,w)\) is the normalized KDE for \(\chi\)-bin \(k\), the conditional model is

\[ p_{\rm mod}(w\mid u)= \frac{\frac1K\sum_k f_k(u,w)} {\frac1K\sum_k f_k^u(u)} =\sum_k \underbrace{\frac{f_k^u(u)}{\sum_j f_j^u(u)}}_{\Pr(k\mid u)} \frac{f_k(u,w)}{f_k^u(u)}. \]

That weighting is consequential: at a given \(u\), overlapping \(\chi\) bins contribute according to their model support there. It cancels the mixture’s marginal density in \(u\), but it does not make the mixture weights independent of the \(\chi\!\to u\) mapping. That is the right result if the intended prior over bins is equal before conditioning. If instead the desired branch proportions should reflect particle counts or physical debris density, equal bin weights are the wrong prior. The current scorer explicitly uses equal bin weights. score.py:159–160, score.py:195–202

I would retain the \(\chi\)-binned mixture for now, but compare it against a pooled, \(u\)-local KDE. The mixture can keep distinct branches visible; pooling all particles in a \(\phi_1\) bin is simpler and can be less noisy, but can blur branches or let the densest branch dominate. The mixture’s weakness is sparse bins: each retained bin gets equal prior weight even if it barely meets nmin, and the current bandwidth depends on that bin’s particle count. score.py:166–176

Make the background conditional in \(w\). A simple fixed mixture is [ L_i=(1-\epsilon)p_{\rm mod}(w_i\mid u_i)+\epsilon p_{\rm bg}(w_i), ] where \(p_{\rm bg}(w)\) is normalized over the scored \(w\)-dimensions. But fixed \(\epsilon\) is not the conditional form of a joint model/background mixture. For that, define a joint background \(g(u,w)=g_u(u)g_w(w)\), and use [ L_i = \frac{(1-\epsilon)f(u_i,w_i)+\epsilon g_u(u_i)g_w(w_i)} {(1-\epsilon)f_u(u_i)+\epsilon g_u(u_i)}. ] This keeps the ratio defined where model support is tiny and makes the background fraction rise where the model has little support. Choose \(g_u\) over the actual analysis interval or selection window. Do not rescue a tiny denominator with an arbitrary floor and then call the result a normalized conditional density.

A concrete API would be:

score_chi_kde_conditional(
    data, model, u_data, u_model, w_data, w_model,
    dchi=5., chi_max=None, nmin=20, age_max=700.,
    bandwidths=..., eps=0.05, bg_u=..., bg_w=...,
)

Have u and w supplied explicitly so the path projection and scored dimensions are reviewable. Compute each bin’s joint density and \(u\)-marginal with a consistent KDE; evaluate the final ratio and background sum in log space. The existing scorer builds the KDE from fixed l,b,pmra,pmdec columns and adds Gaia PM covariance, but does not project through either path or condition on \(u\). score.py:161–165, score.py:178–195

Keep the sum over members as the default. More members in a region normally mean more evidence there; normalizing each \(u\)-bin’s data contribution would change the target from the observed sample likelihood to an approximately equal-bin scoring rule. If the concern is correlated members, calibrate uncertainty by resampling along-stream blocks rather than assigning every star equal independent information. The code sums per-star log likelihoods. score.py:197–202

For the coordinate, I would start with chord-GC \(\phi_1\) for the primary published comparison and treat spline \(s\) as a sensitivity analysis. That is a pragmatic choice, not a conclusion that GC is better conditioned near the cluster. The spline projection is nearest-point based, and its \(s\) is arc length along the path; the GC projection uses a rotated longitude and polynomial-subtracted cross-track coordinate. Both can make off-path or ambiguous projections problematic. path.py:67–77, path.py:127–130

The packet’s near-cluster width and extent summaries favor the spline’s narrower projection there, but they are not independently verified here. In that broad, lumpy region, either single-path coordinate may assign \(u\) arbitrarily; test the score with a predeclared near-cluster exclusion or a separate broad component. Also, the provided path-building scripts derive the spline from member positions and build the GC frame from that ridge. Using those data-derived paths to score the same members risks using the data twice; freeze the path from independent data or use cross-fitting. build_stream_path.py:14–17, build_gc_frame.py:15–21

Handle finite \(u\)-range edges explicitly: define the analysis interval, use a boundary-corrected KDE or exclude a bandwidth-sized edge region, and report the support/background fraction by \(u\). GC longitude is angular and needs wrap-safe handling at its discontinuity; spline endpoint extension does not guarantee that distant off-path points project sensibly. path.py:43–64, path.py:103–105

For calibration, first freeze bandwidths across model comparisons; the current implementation estimates robust bandwidths from each bin’s particle count and spread, with floors and caps. Then compare a small bandwidth grid, repeat the best candidates with independent spray seeds as well as common random numbers, and use along-stream block resampling of members to measure score variability. Report score differences alongside the spread across those perturbations, rather than treating raw \(\Delta\ln L\) as decisive. score.py:168–176

One concrete edge case to cover before relying on the result: if no \(\chi\) bin survives filtering, K=0; the subsequent mean, argmax, and indexing operations do not provide a valid background-only result. Add explicit handling and tests. score.py:166–180, score.py:195–202

docs.title: Verified in code vs assumed
docs.text:
Verified: score_chi_kde uses \(\chi\) bins, equal bin weights, a robust option with per-bin bandwidth estimation, Gaia PM covariance, and a per-star sum of log likelihoods. The path code provides the stated spline and GC projection functions. The path-building scripts use member data to build those paths. score.py:151–202, path.py:43–77, path.py:127–144

Assumed from the packet: the sample size, stream-membership context, 29 radial velocities, path width/extent summaries, and observed noise/likelihood roughness. I have not independently inspected their input data or reproduced those measurements.

docs.title: Strongest argument against this recommendation
docs.text: Conditioning on an estimated \(u\) can discard real information about the model’s along-stream structure, including the very pile-ups or gaps that may distinguish dynamical models. Equal \(\chi\)-bin priors also impose a deliberate weighting that may not represent the physical stream. If the observed member selection function and particle sampling are understood well enough, a calibrated joint likelihood may be more informative than conditioning away \(u\).

docs.title: What I would check to be sure
docs.text:
• Validate both \(u\) projections on held-out members and model particles, especially near the cluster, at both ends, and wherever the path turns or approaches itself.
  • Compare conditional and pooled-\(u\) KDEs on mock sprays with known branch structure and known \(u\)-density.
  • Test support handling, zero surviving bins, coordinate wrapping, and the background’s normalization and units.
  • Verify how STREAMFINDER selection and member dependence affect the effective sample size.
  • Confirm whether score_chi_kde has dedicated tests; I did not find matching tests in the inspected test search.

docs.title: Codex review: score cutoff speed-up and mock-data design (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only. Adopted: absolute-error tests on real sprays (cutoff 7), full-count normalisation, one-pass group jackknife, mock support redraw (measured), fixed-bin weights, several truth seeds/catalogues, independent scores at truth and maxima, angle-10 truth moved inside, per-mock output directories.

B is not directly compatible with the current scorer: foreground Gaussian draws can leave BG_BOUNDS or V_BOUNDS, and the scorer then raises instead of assigning zero background density. Rejecting or clipping those draws would change the proposed distribution. Fix that before calling the mock exact. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:265–279)

A: implement the cutoff, starting at 6, with an error budget and exact fallback.

  1. Highest priority: correct the error claim. A sky-only cut is sufficient to bound the absolute omitted density, assuming valid covariance matrices and positive bandwidths. The PM Gaussian is bounded by its peak, which can exceed one. Thus an excluded joint contribution is bounded by [ e^{-c^2/2}\big/[(2\pi h_u h_x)(2\pi\sqrt{\det\Sigma_i})], ] multiplied by the velocity peak when measured. This is relative to the kernel’s peak, not relative to the retained density or likelihood. The implemented normalisations require those factors. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:306–324)

Far particles can supply essentially all foreground density. Background dominance limits the resulting log error only when the omitted numerator is small relative to the background floor; “small foreground” alone is insufficient. Truncating f_u also changes the denominator, so score error can have either sign. Bound both errors against their respective mixture terms and enlarge the cutoff or fall back when necessary. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:327–329)

  1. Preserve normalisation and empty-bin behaviour. Divide by full n_k, retain fixed K, and compute the u marginal independently of x. Fixed-edge bins retain empty-bin weights; legacy bins discard bins below nmin; pooled scoring has its own minimum-count rule. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:282–305) Sum squared weighted contributions for n_eff. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:323–334)

  2. Vectorise after measuring neighbour occupancy. Chunked flattened member/particle pairs with bincount(minlength=...) avoid reduceat’s empty-segment traps. Bound pair-array memory. A further opportunity is accumulating kernel sums by jackknife group once, then reconstructing leave-outs with adjusted bin counts: the present jackknife recomputes the complete score ten times. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score_bias.py:82–91)

  3. Test absolute log errors, not relative totals. Keep cutoff=None bit-identical. For finite cutoffs, suggested initial gates are maximum per-star error <10⁻⁵ and total error <0.1, including the corrected total; tighten if scientifically relevant differences are smaller. Jackknife can amplify bounded constituent errors by up to 19 for G=10. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score_bias.py:75–91)

Cover pooled/fixed/legacy bins, sparse and empty bins, cutoff boundaries, zero neighbours, correlated PM errors, measured/missing velocities, components and n_eff. Existing score tests exercise binning and n_eff, but their fixtures lack measured velocities and correlated PM covariance. (tests/test_score_conditional.py:9–14, tests/test_score_conditional.py:97–137) Test density errors separately where background dominance makes log errors insensitive.

B: the sampling algebra is correct for the raw finite-spray conditional KDE, after resolving support and matching binning.

  1. Match the actual training target. Training uses fixed edges 0:5:200; the old generator dynamically drops bins with fewer than 20 particles. Do not reuse its prep() unchanged. Use 1/(K n_k) for occupied fixed bins, retain empty-bin weights in f_u, and normalise the particle-selection probabilities only when sampling the foreground. (bin/streams/training_set.py:58, bin/streams/d2_mock_recovery.py:24–29, src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:288–295)

Your background probability and Gaussian covariance then reproduce the raw conditional formula. They do not generate exactly from an infinite-particle model or a normalised jackknife-corrected likelihood; jackknife adjusts log scores. (src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:308–328, src/ocen_dm/streams/score_bias.py:91)

  1. Keep real u, errors and velocity availability. That is appropriate for conditional recovery, assuming selection and missingness can be treated as fixed. It does not validate those assumptions. Freeze the real background bounds rather than estimating them from each mock; the current bounds are derived from real observations. (bin/streams/grid4_common.py:15–18, bin/streams/grid4_common.py:86–89) Specify truth PMRA and PMDEC too: the emulator is nine-dimensional. (bin/streams/emulator_design.py:29–39)

  2. Separate recovery from emulator calibration. Independent truth seeds make this a useful internal closure test, but shared simulator physics cannot establish physical correctness. Use several truth-spray seeds and mock catalogues. Start at matching particle count, then increase truth particles until recovery conclusions stabilise.

Reject “within 1000 of peak” and training-point rank as primary acceptance criteria. Calibrate likelihood-ratio regions across repeated mocks; independently score truth and proposed maxima to distinguish interpolation failure from sampling variation. Separately assess held-out score residuals using predictive plus simulation variance, as the current validation does. (bin/streams/emulator_design.py:107–140) The angle-10 truth lies on the design boundary, so symmetric parameter-error criteria are inappropriate. (bin/streams/emulator_design.py:36)

  1. Protect results. Write mock scores to separate directories with catalogue hash, truth seed, cutoff and likelihood settings. The emulator loader consumes total_jk and var_jk; it checks simulation identity and within-batch manifest consistency, but does not explicitly enforce a common mock-catalogue identity across batches. (bin/streams/emulator_design.py:43–81)

1. Verified versus assumed. Verified by reading all five requested files and the cited training/tests: formulas, support rejection, binning, correction and loading behaviour. Mathematical bounds above are deductions assuming finite inputs, positive bandwidths and valid covariances. I did not verify the stated timings, spray counts or realised recovery performance, and ran no tests.

2. Strongest argument against this recommendation. Six bandwidths may already make errors negligible on every relevant spray; fallback machinery could add complexity without measurable benefit. Conversely, a few successful closure mocks could conceal poor recovery elsewhere.

3. Needed for confidence. Exact-versus-cutoff benchmarks on representative and deliberately mismatched sprays; corrected-score error and memory measurements; generator normalisation/support tests; independent scores around recovered maxima; repeated-mock coverage; and particle-count/seed convergence. Existing jackknife and emulator tests establish toy behaviour, not this end-to-end recovery. (tests/test_score_bias.py:30–44, tests/test_emulator.py:8–41)

docs.title: Codex diagnostic experiments 2026 10 10
docs.text: The premise is broadly consistent with the code. One qualification: the grid’s \(16^\circ\) result is a raw likelihood maximum, not a fit with the stated \(N(27^\circ,2^\circ)\) prior; grid4.py scores each grid point without adding a prior, while the separate fit script defines that prior and bounds angle to \(21–33^\circ\) (grid4.py:20–41; fit_bar_ocen.py:26–35).

docs.title: 1. The knee is too shallow and the model thins out
docs.text:
1. Spray release and selection mismatch — high plausibility. The spray uses a Fardal-style release prescription, but the fit selects model particles by arm, age, and \(\chi\), not by a STREAMFINDER detection or membership process (spray.py:42–64; score.py:250–253). The observed catalogue is filtered by stream label and sky cuts (spray_bar_grid2.py:24–31). This could explain the apparent thinning without explaining a coherent proper-motion offset.

  2. The barred host or its history is too simple — high plausibility. The host supports a constant pattern speed, present angle, and scaled barred-baryon component (restricted.py:40–61). A mismatch in bar history or shape can affect the outer-tail track and knee together.

  3. Centre-orbit state or frame conversion — moderate plausibility. The grid fixes the cluster PMs and uses discrete distances; the centre state is built from those values (grid4_common.py:14–30). A small present-day state error can accumulate along a long integrated orbit.

  4. Release window or age cut — moderate-to-low plausibility. Releases cover the last 1000 Myr, and scoring drops particles at age \(700\) Myr (grid4_common.py:25–30; score.py:250–253). This can remove outer-tail support if the relevant debris is older, but it cannot by itself explain a systematic PM offset in debris that remains.

docs.title: 2. Bar angle is implausibly low and near the grid edge
docs.text:
1. The model is compensating for an omitted ingredient — high plausibility. The angle, amplitude, pattern speed, and distance vary together in the grid, while PMs and cluster radial velocity are held fixed (grid4.py:20–40). The code does not establish that the angle itself is identifiable when those assumptions are fixed.
  2. Likelihood or frame construction favors the knee over the inner stream — high plausibility. The score conditions on observed along-stream coordinate and gives equal prior weight to valid \(\chi\) bins (score.py:233–245). The adopted frame is a fixed chord frame with a fitted polynomial track (path.py:133–144); its stored maximum ridge deviation is \(1.071^\circ\) (stream54_gc_frame_chord.json:10–26).
  3. The constant-speed bar prescription is incomplete — moderate plausibility. host_potential encodes constant pattern speed and a specific scaled difference between barred and axisymmetrised baryons (restricted.py:40–61).
  4. A true preference for \(16^\circ\) — possible, but not established. The supplied block-bootstrap and seed results already indicate that the raw difference is unstable; the code’s grid itself does not impose the literature-angle prior (grid4.py:20–41; seed_test.py:11–30; bootstrap_grid4.py:19–48).

docs.title: 3. Statistics are overconfident or unstable
docs.text:
1. Sparse local particle support — high plausibility. Each \(\chi\) bin is a KDE over spray particles, and only bins with at least 20 particles are retained (score.py:250–272). The diagnostic computes effective particle count from the same kernel weights (kernel_check.py:25–40).
  2. Correlated members treated as independent — high plausibility. The likelihood sums a per-member log likelihood (score.py:273–275); the bootstrap code explicitly contrasts iid resampling with contiguous \(\phi_1\) blocks (bootstrap_grid4.py:2–7).
  3. A fixed bandwidth and background share alter model ranking — moderate-to-high plausibility. The conditional KDE uses fixed bandwidths and a fixed eps=0.05 background mixture (score.py:231–245). The existing bandwidth diagnostic rescales widths, but that is a sensitivity check, not a calibrated uncertainty model (kernel_check.py:49–57).
  4. The grid maximum is a noisy boundary result — high plausibility. Angle is sampled only at \(16,20,24,28^\circ\) in the reported grid (grid4.py:20); selecting the maximum among many noisy points adds a winner’s-curse effect.

docs.title: 4. Dark-matter effects are missed by the adopted score
docs.text:
1. Along-stream counts are deliberately discarded — certain from code. The score forms a conditional density by dividing the joint KDE by its along-stream marginal and uses equal weights across valid \(\chi\) bins (score.py:233–245, 261–275). It is therefore not a test of DM-driven escape counts.
  2. The tested grid fixes the progenitor profile to A_nodm — high plausibility. The grid loads that profile for all models (grid4_common.py:19; grid4.py:26).
  3. Selection confounds count comparisons — high plausibility. The observed sample is catalogue-selected and sky-filtered (spray_bar_grid2.py:24–31); a count likelihood needs a defensible model of detection and membership completeness before count differences can be attributed to DM.

docs.title: Q2. Prioritised experiments
docs.text:
Costs below use the supplied timings: about 11 seconds for an 8000-epoch spray, 45 seconds for 32000 epochs, and 11.5 minutes for a 200k tracer run, each at the stated 8-thread setup. They are approximate and exclude plotting and setup. The 4D grid has \(7×4×4×4=448\) points, or about 82 minutes of spray time at 11 seconds each, before overhead.

  1. Audit coordinates, bar clock, and release-time Jacobi radii. Hypothesis: a sign, clock, or numerical error is manufacturing some of the bar-angle preference or knee mismatch. Design: no grid. For a representative orbit and release times, compare the bar angle evaluated at \(t=0,T\) with the requested present angle; compare rj_vj_R’s directional second derivative against a finite-difference radial-force derivative at several orbit phases; forward-integrate the reconstructed centre orbit and report present-day position and velocity residuals. Also project data and representative sprays through the stored chord frame and a pole-fit frame. Diagnostic / decision: plot angle versus time, \(r_J\) residuals versus orbital phase, orbit round-trip residuals, and \(\Delta\phi_2\) between frames. A systematic sign or phase error, or release-radius discrepancy large enough to move the stream track, confirms an implementation concern. Cost: negligible to minutes; no new spray required. The relevant code evaluates the host at each release time and reconstructs the centre orbit backward then forward (spray.py:22–39, 107–119; restricted.py:40–61).

  2. Rescore existing sprays by segment and observable. Hypothesis: the low angle is driven mainly by the knee, while inner-stream and other-observable scores prefer a different model. Design: reuse cached sprays at the best \(16^\circ\) point and at \(20,24,28^\circ\), including the best available amplitude, pattern speed, and distance for each. Report per-star \(\Delta\ln L\) and median/ridge residuals separately over \(\phi_1=-2..4\), \(4..17\), and \(17..27^\circ\), and separately for sky offset, PMs, and radial velocity. Do not change bandwidths or data cuts. Diagnostic / decision: segment score table plus residual-versus-\(\phi_1\) plots. If angle preference reverses by segment or observable, prioritize model inadequacy over further global optimization. Cost: scoring existing files; likely minutes, no new spray.

  3. Mock injection and recovery of the score and grid. Hypothesis: the score or finite particle support systematically recovers low angles even when the generating model has a literature-like angle. Design: take cached sprays at \(28^\circ\) and \(20^\circ\) as separate truths. Generate 100 catalogues of 3681 mock members from each truth, with the observed \(\phi_1\) distribution held fixed, Gaia PM covariances and the observed radial-velocity missingness/error pattern applied. Score each mock against cached candidate models. Repeat with 8000- and 32000-epoch truth sprays if available; hold the grid and score widths fixed. Diagnostic / decision: recovery histograms for angle and \(\Delta\ln L(16-20)\), plus calibration of nominal score separation. If mocks generated at \(28^\circ\) often recover \(16^\circ\), the current ranking is not trustworthy under its own assumptions. If recovery is accurate, the explanation likely lies in model mismatch or data selection. Cost: no new sprays if cached; scoring 200 mock catalogues may take from minutes to hours depending on implementation. This estimate needs a short timing run before committing.

  4. Free the cluster state locally at fixed literature-like bar angle. Hypothesis: fixed cluster PMs, rather than bar angle, are forcing the knee and inner stream into conflict. Design: at angle \(28^\circ\), pattern speed \(34.5\), amplitude \(1.2\), distance \(5.5\) kpc, compare catalogue PMs with the grid PMs \((-3.2223,-6.7517)\), plus each PM shifted by \(\pm0.027\) mas/yr individually. Hold \(v_{\rm los}\) fixed as the existing fit does; use common release epochs and seed. Use the conditional score, and report the PM prior penalty separately rather than hiding it in the likelihood. Diagnostic / decision: a 2D PM score map and segment residuals. If plausible PM shifts materially improve both inner and knee segments while keeping angle near \(28^\circ\), the fixed-state assumption was consequential. Cost: 5 sprays, about 55 seconds plus scoring. The separate fit script already has a PM-free path and Gaussian PM priors (fit_bar_ocen.py:26–35, 51–72).

  5. Calibrate spray against prescribed tracers in the barred host. Hypothesis: the release prescription, not the host orbit, produces the missing tail support or PM curvature. Design: run 200k tracers at a \(28^\circ\) host and the same centre state and progenitor profile as the spray, without spin. Compare age-resolved ridge, counts per 2-degree \(\phi_1\) bin, PM medians, and radial velocity. If time permits, repeat at \(16^\circ\) using identical tracer ICs. Diagnostic / decision: if tracer debris reaches the observed knee while the spray does not at the same host, the release model is implicated. If both miss similarly, the host, orbit, selection, or frame is more likely. Cost: about 11.5 minutes per run by the supplied timing; two runs about 23 minutes. Note that the tracer setup integrates sampled equilibrium stars in a fixed moving satellite potential (run_prescribed.py:73–109), whereas the spray injects particles at release points (spray.py:42–64).

  6. Test release window and age selection. Hypothesis: the knee requires older debris omitted by the 700 Myr age cut or 1000 Myr release window. Design: for the \(16^\circ\) and \(28^\circ\) reference models, keep 8000 epochs and seed 1, extend the release interval to 1500 Myr, and rescore with age limits 500, 700, 1000, and 1500 Myr. Plot the age distribution of particles contributing to each member’s likelihood. Diagnostic / decision: if the knee residual improves only when older debris is admitted, this supports the age/window hypothesis; if not, deprioritize it. Cost: two longer sprays; the supplied 11-second baseline may understate their cost because particles have longer integration times.

  7. Compare constant-speed and decelerating-bar histories. Hypothesis: a different bar history can fit the knee and inner stream without pushing the present angle below the literature range. Design: after the clock/sign audit, compare constant speed to one explicitly parameterized slowing history, matched to the same present-day \(\Omega_b\), present angle \(28^\circ\), and amplitude \(1.2\). Use the same epochs, seed, distance, and cluster state. First run one model per history, then only a small local variation if track residuals improve. Diagnostic / decision: compare segment PM/sky residuals and radial-velocity residuals, not only total conditional score. Improvement confined to one segment is insufficient. Cost: roughly 22 seconds for two baseline sprays, plus any slower-history overhead. Implementing a new history is additional work.

  8. Only then test bar shape and halo/LMC alternatives. Hypothesis: the specific Hunter+2024 bar or fixed axisymmetric halo is inadequate. Design: one alternative bar shape at \(28^\circ\) and one justified halo/LMC variant, matched to the same present centre state and broadly comparable circular-speed curve. Compare with the same observables and segment diagnostics. Diagnostic / decision: proceed to a small follow-up only if an alternative reduces both the knee and inner-stream residuals without relying on the conditional score alone. Cost: about 22 seconds for two baseline sprays, plus model setup; uncertainty is larger because the alternative potentials are not specified in the current code paths.

docs.title: Q3. Before another grid, and when to change the likelihood
docs.text:
Before any new grid, I would run experiments 1–4: verify time/frame mechanics, determine which segments drive the angle result, check recovery bias, and test whether the fixed cluster state matters. These are cheap and separate numerical or statistical effects from physical model error.

I would change the likelihood only if mock recovery is biased, the selected bandwidth/background materially changes the ranking, or the current conditional objective answers the wrong scientific question. In particular, if the question is about DM-driven escape counts, add a count term only after modeling the catalogue selection and completeness; the current score explicitly conditions out density along the stream (score.py:233–245). I would not treat broader bandwidths or an extra error floor as a fix: the current score has fixed widths and a 5% background component (score.py:231–245), and any new uncertainty model should be calibrated by mock recovery first.

docs.title: Q4. Code-path weaknesses and checks
docs.text:
Verified in code:

  • host_potential sets the angle to \(\theta_{\rm today}+\Omega_b(t-t_{\rm today})\), with \(\Omega_b\) supplied in km/s/kpc and the angle in radians (restricted.py:40–55). The units are consistent if the time coordinate is AGAMA’s kpc/(km/s) unit, as the module states (restricted.py:14–15); I have not independently verified AGAMA’s rotation convention against the potential assets.
  • rj_vj_R passes release times to host.eval, computes a radial second derivative from the returned derivative components, clips the Jacobi denominator to \(10^{-6}\), and runs 30 fixed-point updates without a convergence check (spray.py:22–39). This deserves the finite-difference audit: a derivative layout, sign, or near-zero denominator error would alter release radii and thus stream length.
  • The centre orbit is integrated backward from today and then forward; the second integration samples the centre track every 0.05 Myr for the moving satellite potential (spray.py:107–119). This is a reasonable construction, but the stream code does not itself assert that the forward endpoint returns to the specified present state; the prescribed-tracer script records a centre offset (run_prescribed.py:100–104, 120–126).
  • The chord-frame projection uses atan2 stream longitude and subtracts a polynomial \(\phi_2(\phi_1)\) (path.py:127–130). The stored frame spans \(\phi_1\approx-1.8..26.9^\circ\) and has max_dev \(1.071^\circ\) (stream54_gc_frame_chord.json:10–26). That does not prove it is a bad frame, but it is enough to justify rechecking near-cluster and knee residuals in an independent frame.
  • The focused conditional-score tests cover background-only behavior, cancellation of along-stream density, duplicated bins, and a deliberately wrong PM model (test_score_conditional.py:24–65). The focused spray-spin tests check the sign and geometry of the added spin velocity (test_spray_spin.py:14–30); these tests do not establish bar-clock, Jacobi-radius, or end-to-end barred-orbit correctness.
  • score_conditional uses a fixed mixture fraction, fixed widths, Gaussian PM covariance, and a finite uniform background box; it does not validate positive covariance determinants or adapt the model bandwidth to local particle support (score.py:231–275). Sparse support can therefore affect the score before the background component dominates.

Assumptions: I take the packet’s stated bar-angle literature range, timing measurements, tail residuals, and prior bootstrap/seed results as inputs; I did not reproduce them. I also assume the catalogue selection and the external Hunter potential assets are as described in the packet.

Strongest argument against my top recommendation: The mock-injection/recovery experiment can be circular. If mocks are generated from the same spray prescription, frame, and score being tested, successful recovery only shows internal self-consistency; it cannot show that the prescription resembles the real stream. That is why I would pair it with the barred-host tracer comparison before drawing a physical conclusion.

What I would still need to check to be sure: the AGAMA eval(..., der=True) component ordering and time semantics against a finite-difference oracle; forward/backward orbit residuals for the actual best-fit states; frame sensitivity of the segment results; mock-recovery behavior with realistic catalogue selection; and whether tracer-versus-spray differences persist across at least one seed and the two relevant bar angles.

docs.title: Q1. Parallax offset
docs.text:
The script does not establish that STREAMFINDER’s parallax term caused the offset. It selects the stream sample from the STREAMFINDER catalogue, crossmatches Gaia parallaxes, and calculates inverse-variance weighted means; it does not compare that sample with a cluster sample matched in magnitude, colour, astrometric quality, or sky position (parallax_check.py:19–21, 26–39). It applies a single assumed zero-point band, not per-star corrections (parallax_check.py:4–5, 38–40).

The stated stream offset from the models survives that global correction: the stored weighted mean at phi1 < 4 is 0.228 mas, versus about 0.179 mas predicted by the models; adding 0.017 mas to the observed mean increases the difference (parallax_check.json:2–13). But those reported errors are just \(1/\sqrt{\sum 1/\sigma^2}\); the code does not include correlated or selection-related uncertainty (parallax_check.py:31–39).

Two cheap discriminating checks:

  • Match the cluster and stream samples in Gaia G, BP−RP, RUWE, parallax uncertainty, and relevant astrometric-quality cuts; compare corrected parallax distributions and repeat in cluster radius bins. If the discrepancy tracks cluster radius or crowding, the cluster comparison is suspect; if it remains in matched samples, a stream-selection or population explanation becomes more plausible.
  • Recalculate the stream parallax trend using an independent PM/sky-selected sample, with the same Gaia quality cuts and per-star zero-point treatment. The current parallax script reuses STREAMFINDER membership, so it cannot test whether that selection drives the result (parallax_check.py:19–21, 26–30).

docs.title: Q2. CMD track
docs.text:
I would not use this as a distance calibration. The fitted shifts are a useful consistency clue, but the normalization is incomplete for the stated CMD window. Stars are selected within both colour and magnitude bounds (stream54_cmd_distance.py:28, 50–52); the likelihood then corrects only for the shifted reference stars passing the upper G limit (stream54_cmd_distance.py:38–42). It does not normalize for the lower G boundary or colour selection. The fit also jointly allows a colour shift, making distance and residual reddening/calibration partially interchangeable (stream54_cmd_distance.py:30–31, 37–43).

The reported trend is present in the output: for example, the b=36–39 bin has a distance ratio of 0.879, while b=33–36 gives 0.920 (stream54_cmd_distance.json:53–78). But bins are in Galactic latitude, not the fit’s chord-frame phi1, so mapping those values onto the PM knee needs checking (stream54_cmd_distance.py:29, 65–73). The injection and split-half checks validate recovery under the script’s own synthetic shifts; they do not test a template-dependent catalogue selection or changing stellar populations (stream54_cmd_distance.py:53–61). Also, the docstring says 200 bootstrap resamples, but the code uses 50 (stream54_cmd_distance.py:5–6, 69).

The cheap check is to compare the fitted shift with the same magnitude-only fit already computed, inspect whether best fits accumulate at the dm or dc grid edges, and repeat with narrower interior colour/magnitude cuts. If the trend changes materially, discard it as a distance indicator. The current output already shows some joint versus magnitude-only differences, especially in b=39–42 (stream54_cmd_distance.json:80–92).

docs.title: Q3. Distance-free likelihood
docs.text:
Yes, it is defensible as a conditional fit to the observed stream track and kinematics, not as a complete dynamical constraint. The implemented score conditions on observed along-stream coordinate \(u\), and scores cross-stream position, PMs, and available radial velocities; it intentionally removes along-stream density (score.py:231–245, 273–275). That avoids treating uncertain observed distances as data in the score. It does not make the model independent of distance: the predicted PMs and sky positions still come from model particles generated from an assumed progenitor phase-space point (grid4_common.py:40–49, 52–54).

The cost is that this score cannot use along-stream density or directly constrain the distance gradient. Distance, transverse velocity, solar reflex, and orbit geometry can compensate for one another; bar and halo effects that produce similar projected PM/track changes remain harder to distinguish. A relative parallax difference along the stream could still help if samples are selected and quality-matched across bins and zero-point variation is controlled. A raw parallax ratio is less safe when the zero point is additive. Radial velocities are already included when present, but the loader accepts only 29 finite velocities (spray_bar_grid2.py:29–31); they are a sparse independent constraint, not a replacement for a distance track.

docs.title: Q4. Remaining PM misfit
docs.text:
The most useful untested or incompletely tested discriminants are:

  1. Solar reflex and progenitor distance. The default frame fixes \(R_0=8.178\) kpc and \(V_\odot=(11.1,252.24,7.25)\) km/s; the alternative frame changes both solar parameters and the adopted cluster distance (frames.py:16–20, 23–28). The phase-2b grid instead fixes the progenitor at 5.6 kpc (phase2b_grid.py:34). Run a small controlled grid over the two frames and 5.43/5.6 kpc, comparing per-star PM residuals in the knee. This is my first test because it directly probes a shared source of PM shifts.

  2. Angle–pattern-speed coupling with the longer bar. The longer-bar extension varies \(\Omega_b\), size, and amplitude at fixed \(28^\circ\) (phase2b_grid.py:14–21, 34). A compact grid combining the preferred lower angles with the longer-bar settings would show whether the reported \(16^\circ\) preference persists after those ingredients are coupled. Avoid interpreting a best point at the edge of the sampled \(\Omega_b\) range as a settled optimum.

  3. LMC forcing and progenitor mass history. The stream runs construct a Hunter barred host and spray particles using one fixed A_nodm enclosed-mass profile (grid4_common.py:19, 40–49). In the spray, the satellite potential is built from that fixed profile and carried along the centre orbit (spray.py:113–119). A controlled LMC-plus-reflex run and a small set of alternative progenitor profiles would test whether either missing ingredient can move the two PM tracks in the required directions. These are more expensive than the frame grid, so I would run them after it.

A spline-path frame comparison is already implemented, so “the stream frame” is not wholly untested; the script compares chord and one fixed spline path (knee_spread_and_frame.py:7–9, 47–56). The supplied files do not establish whether path uncertainty or alternative membership cuts were tested.

docs.title: Verified versus assumed
docs.text:
Verified by reading code and stored outputs: the parallax script’s sample construction, global zero-point band, weighted-mean calculation, and model comparison; the CMD fit’s selection cuts, partial truncation correction, joint colour shift, actual 50 bootstrap resamples, and stored ratios; and the conditional score’s inputs and conditioning on \(u\) (parallax_check.py:19–46, stream54_cmd_distance.py:28–43, 65–73, score.py:231–245, 273–275).

Assumed from the packet, not independently verified here: the cluster-sample parallax statistics, the quoted likelihood preferences and PM residuals, and the claimed outcomes of the earlier diagnostic experiments. The packet’s claim that the fit uses a distance-free likelihood is accurate only in the conditional-score sense described above.

docs.title: Strongest argument against my answer
docs.text: The CMD code recovers its injected magnitude and colour shift, and the larger-\(b\) bins show a coherent brightening trend (stream54_cmd_distance.py:58–61, 69–73; stream54_cmd_distance.json:53–78). If STREAMFINDER’s selection is sufficiently uniform within the fitted CMD window and the stellar populations are similar, the trend may be real and useful qualitatively. Likewise, the parallax offset remains after the script’s central global zero-point adjustment (parallax_check.json:2–13). The missing evidence is whether either result survives matched selection and systematics, not whether the numerical trend appears in the stored output.

docs.title: What I would check to be sure
docs.text:
• The exact construction and quality cuts for the cluster parallax sample, plus per-star Gaia zero-point and colour/magnitude matching.
  • Whether the CMD bins map to the quoted PM-knee phi1 interval, and whether the shift survives interior-window and magnitude-only fits.
  • The phase-2b and frame-comparison result tables, including whether the relevant parameter optima sit at grid edges.
  • A small joint grid varying solar frame/progenitor distance with bar angle and pattern speed before spending effort on LMC or progenitor-profile runs.

docs.title: Codex review: low-angle bias of the emulator in the mock recovery test (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only.

The “exactly the real-data pipeline” premise is false: mock recovery adds the true parameters as an optimizer start and optimizes its profiles; the real-data report starts from measured points and constructs profiles from a finite candidate set. This makes the mock search more informed, yet T2 still fails. (mock_recovery.py:80–111, emulator_report.py:75–100)

My recommendation: retain GPs to guide simulations, but use angle-stratified, multi-start local searches with independently checked profile values. Do not infer bar-angle uncertainty from the current global GP. T2c1 now confirms T2c0: angle error −15.9°, truth residual 5.92σ. (T2c1 recovery.json:55–112)

The roots, in order of confidence:

  1. Missing high-likelihood joint coverage is demonstrated. For T2c0, the independent truth check beats every fitted training run by 1,954; for T2c1, by 2,027. Neither catalogue supplies the emulator with observations near the known high score. Marginal angle-bin counts cannot establish coverage of a coupled nine-dimensional ridge. Moreover, 488 sprays mean 375 distinct fitted locations, 470 fitted runs and 18 held-out runs—not 488 independent locations. (T2c0 recovery.json:14–64, T2c1 recovery.json:55–64, mock_recovery.py:54–66)

  2. The acquisition policy can reinforce this gap. It adds candidates around the ten highest measured scores, then selects by global \(\mu+2\sigma\); batch uncertainty updates keep the fitted kernel fixed. An underestimated alternative ridge can therefore lose both exploitation and uncertainty-driven exploration. The mechanism exists; its causal contribution needs an ablation. (emulator_design.py:161–193)

  3. Predictive uncertainty fails where it matters; the proposed explanation remains unproved. T2’s top-quintile coverage is already only 79%, versus 91% globally. “Globally calibrated” conceals a visible failure. The implementation conditions on fitted kernel and noise parameters; it does not propagate their uncertainty. But the results do not distinguish nonstationarity, a poorly aligned kernel metric, mean misspecification or inadequate observations. (T2c0 recovery.json:17–33, emulator.py:40–79)

  4. Constant-mean reversion is real, but not an established diagnosis. The GP subtracts the unweighted mean of distinct-point scores. Recomputing that mean gives −34,136 for T2c0—not approximately −27,000. Its prediction at truth, −27,244, is substantially above that mean. Shrinkage may suppress the peak, but “it returned to the ensemble mean” is inaccurate here. (emulator.py:25–34,68–79, T2c0 rescore.json:1, T2c0 recovery.json:55–61)

  5. There is a separate mock-target issue. Catalogues are sampled from one finite spray’s raw KDE, whereas the emulator targets jackknife-corrected scores from independent sprays. Generating-spray self-scores exceed independent checks by roughly 528–741 across these four catalogues. That does not explain away a 5,070-point interpolation error, but it prevents treating the experiment as exact recovery from the infinite-particle target. Both catalogues at a truth also share that generating spray. (mock_data.py:59–85,99–105, emulator.py:5–6, T1c0 recovery.json:55–61, T1c1 recovery.json:55–61, T2c0 recovery.json:55–61, T2c1 recovery.json:55–61)

Ranked work programme

  1. First, benchmark using existing scores. Compare Sobol-only against the full design, retaining grouped replicates. Use blocked validation by angle–Ω region and joint neighbourhood, alongside random folds. Compare constant, linear and regularized quadratic means with GP residuals; refit everything inside each fold. Score performance on independent truth checks, high-score holdouts and likelihood differences, not aggregate RMSE alone. Current CV randomly partitions the existing locations, so it does not test discovery of an omitted ridge. (emulator_design.py:107–123)

Also perform an explicitly oracle diagnostic: add the already available truth-check observation and refit. If the fitted peak moves sharply, that establishes sensitivity to missing information. It is not an acceptance test.

  1. Spend the next simulation budget on stratified local search. Start with approximately 100 runs at 128k: 80 distributed across five angle anchors and separated nuisance-parameter starts, plus 20 global discovery runs. Adapt in small batches; share observations between neighbouring angles rather than fitting isolated eight-dimensional GPs to tiny samples. Promote perhaps 20 competitive points to independent 256k checks. At your supplied timings, that is about 14 core-hours, before replication and fitting.

Test this first on failing T2 with the same budget and stopping rules intended for real data, without truth-informed starts. Local trust-region BO is a defensible approach to heterogeneous objectives; it is not a guarantee of finding every mode. (TuRBO paper)

  1. Use quadratic means as a cheap challenger, not the main cure. A full quadratic has 55 coefficients in nine dimensions: regularize it and include coefficient uncertainty. It can describe a rotated broad ridge; it cannot establish an unobserved narrow peak. Polynomial means plus GP residuals have a standard formulation. (GPML, §2.7)

  2. Defer blanket densification and hard partitions. Another 300–500 runs at 128k costs 30–50 core-hours. Under uniform nine-dimensional spacing, that improves nominal spacing by only about 6–9% relative to 375 locations. Prefer a targeted pilot with measurable improvement before buying that expansion.

Before mixing resolutions, calibrate 128k versus 256k at newly found competitive points. Existing documented convergence checks cover two calibration locations and have uncertainty around 35; they do not establish resolution equivalence on every mock ridge. The current loader also explicitly rejects non-256k runs, so mixed-resolution fitting requires a deliberate change. (stream_status.md:73–79, emulator_design.py:51–57)

Acceptance criteria

  • Search: the independently checked best candidate must not score materially below the known truth check. Use a predeclared search tolerance—say 100 log-score units initially—and replicate enough to resolve that comparison. This is necessary, not sufficient.
  • Surrogate: validate profile differences near competing modes and interval boundaries. For inference using \(\exp(\ell/T)\), target numerical errors well below \(T\), for example \(0.2T\). If unattainable at \(T=1\), precise raw-likelihood inference is unsupported. Tempering needs statistical justification, not selection to conceal emulator error.
  • Recovery: test angles 12/20/27/33, weak bars and nuisance placements away from the explored ridge. Compare against independently evaluated optima; do not require the finite-sample optimum to equal the generating parameters.
  • Coverage: use repeated catalogues and independent generating sprays. Assess nominal interval coverage with binomial uncertainty, separately by truth regime. Weak-bar tests may correctly return broad angle intervals. Neither two catalogues nor a pointwise GP band establishes parameter coverage; current profile bands are simply the GP standard deviation at each selected maximizer. (mock_recovery.py:109–112)
  • Pipeline integrity: verify catalogue hashes and settings before recovery. The current recovery script reads the supplied mock and rescore independently without checking their association, and overwrites recovery.json. Fix that before expanding the campaign. (mock_recovery.py:51–55,117)

A GP is suitable as a search model here. Nine dimensions alone do not disqualify it. For the immediate angle question, sequential BO within angle strata is preferable to MCMC: sampling the current surrogate would faithfully reproduce its missed peak. Direct-spray MCMC is expensive, and exponentiating an approximately unbiased log score does not produce the unbiased likelihood estimator required for exact pseudo-marginal sampling. The correction currently operates on log totals. (score.py:419–422, Andrieu & Roberts)

  1. Verified versus assumed. I read the requested implementation and four completed recovery files, and recomputed grouped counts, means and simulation-identity checks from stored scores. Their catalogue hashes match. I did not rerun GP fits or tests. The emulator unit tests exercise a smooth quadratic toy and broad CV coverage, not narrow-ridge discovery or end-to-end parameter recovery. Cutoff/jackknife tests establish agreement between scoring implementations, not recovery correctness. The efficiency of local BO and the precise ridge geometry remain assumptions to test. (test_emulator.py:8–41, test_score_cutoff.py:29–47)

  2. Strongest argument against my recommendation. Local searches can miss disconnected modes, and angle stratification still leaves eight nuisance dimensions. A regularized global trend could exploit structure more efficiently and make the existing library adequate with little additional simulation. My recommendation wins only if matched-budget mock experiments demonstrate better independently checked regret and coverage.

  3. Needed for confidence. Matched-budget design/kernel ablations; direct scores at reported emulator maxima; convergence checks on competitive mock points; independent generating-spray repeats; identical blinded recovery/reporting procedures; and validated physical-coordinate profiles. In particular, the current “size” profile fixes the unit coordinate while physical size changes with Ω, \(v_c\) and \(q\), so it is not a fixed-physical-size profile. (mock_recovery.py:98–109, emulator_design.py:36–39)

docs.title: Codex review: conclusions of the 2026-10-18 emulator campaign
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only. All points checked and adopted in docs/kb/stream_status.md; the best_check pooling bug fixed.

The saved evidence contradicts two details: final median noise SD is 65, not 76, and the optimized final maximum has SD 806, not 575. (validation:30, report:1261)

There is also a reporting bug: best_check pools checks from different parameter points while reporting the first point’s parameters and prediction. Do not quote its combined mean or scatter. (emulator_report.py:107–119)

  • (1) “Calibrated” is too strong; “no reliable bar constraints yet” is defensible. Broad predictive coverage looks approximately consistent, but top-quintile bias is +467 and held-out coverage is 16/18. These do not establish calibration near selected maxima. The profiles maximize over finite candidates; their bands are pointwise prediction uncertainties, not uncertainty bands for optimized profiles. Comparing SD with profile height alone also ignores correlated prediction errors. (validation:21–38, emulator_report.py:69–79)

  • (2) Say “these two reference models are indistinguishable at current precision.” Their means differ by approximately 3, with a rough independent-seed standard error of 70. Two seeds each establish neither equivalence nor resolution convergence. They also differ in distance, amplitude and size, so this is not an isolated angle comparison. Existing resolution checks concern two other calibration points. (reference scores:7–10, reference parameters:12–67, stream_status.md:72–78)

  • (3) Approximately +600 is supported at one independently replicated point, not throughout a “best-fit region.” The eight checks give −21,568.5 with seed SD 29.7 and SE 10.5. Its slow bar, large distance and boundary \(v_c\) are candidate properties, not parameter measurements. No distance prior enters the training target. The new predicted maximum additionally hits the PM-declination and halo-flattening bounds; extending only \(v_c\) misses those warnings. (checks:11–18, checked parameters:24–33, score target:99–109, final maximum:1250–1259)

  • (4) The trade-off persists locally. At \(\phi_1=21^\circ\), the PM-declination residual improves from about −0.82 to −0.16, while the sky offset grows from about 0.47° to 1.42°. That supports a remaining mismatch, not an unavoidable trade-off throughout parameter space. The comparison uses the highest-scoring individual run against a 32k reference, so seed selection and unequal resolution remain caveats. (track values:1306–1477, selection:120–134, reference resolution:9–10)

  • (5) Denser local sampling is justified; a local GP is an experiment, not an established remedy. Retain global exploration and fresh validation. Choose tempering using held-out segments or mock coverage, not by making these profiles look restrictive—the stated calibration plan already requires that. (design:175–189, stream_status.md:98–99)

  • Verified versus assumed. I read the implementation and saved records and recomputed the replicate summaries. I assume the recorded simulations and scores reproduce their inputs; I did not rerun sprays, scores or tests.

  • Strongest argument against my caution. The independently checked gain of about 600 is much larger than its measured seed uncertainty. It is credible evidence of an improved score at that point, despite inaccurate emulator localization. (check scores:11–18)

  • Needed for confidence. Check resolution convergence at the winner and both references; validate nearby competitors with fresh seeds; compare profiles after constrained optimization and joint GP uncertainty. Add regression coverage for check grouping and production validation: the existing toy coverage test exercises a different CV function, and held-out validation uses raw jackknife variance whereas campaign CV uses fitted noise. (test_emulator.py:36–41, emulator_design.py:107–139)

docs.title: Codex review: stochastic-kriging emulator and refinement design (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only. All six findings confirmed and fixed in emulator_design.py (stream_batch.py fixes after the replicate batch ends).

The packet understates the replicate campaign: the current default is 64 points × 2 additional runs, and the existing job list contains 128 jobs. Check the remaining workload before relying on the five-hour estimate. stream_batch.py:45, jobs.json:1

I would fix candidate uniqueness before launching. I would use this GP to guide further simulations, but would not yet use it as a posterior likelihood.

Ranked findings

  1. High: the batch can contain unintended duplicate points. Selected candidates remain eligible for every subsequent argmax. Positive fantasy noise leaves residual uncertainty at selected points; reducing their uncertainty does not guarantee they stop winning. Duplicate indices also propagate into the “eight highest-mu points,” potentially concentrating their extra replicates further. Mask selected candidates explicitly and assert the intended number of distinct coordinates before writing jobs. emulator_design.py:91–103

  2. High: loading results bypasses provenance and duplicate protection. The loader accepts matching JSON files without checking manifests, score settings, particle counts, job identities, or artifact hashes. Supplying the same batch twice—or explicitly supplying the automatically included replicate directory—counts identical simulations as independent replicates. Grouping then trusts the key and silently takes its first coordinate. This can corrupt both S2 and s2/r. Validate compatibility, deduplicate simulation identities, and reject inconsistent coordinates within a key. emulator_design.py:41–55, emulator.py:25–34

  3. High for inference: validation does not hold out the complete fitted pipeline. Once replicate fitting activates, the noise surface uses all points before the mean-GP folds are constructed. Held-out replicate scores therefore influence training weights and validation denominators. Refit the noise model inside each fold. This issue does not apply to the reported initial jackknife-only validation. Also, top-region reporting lacks coverage and signed bias; global coverage cannot establish accuracy near the maximum. emulator_design.py:58–78, emulator.py:82–93

  4. Medium: seeds are unique within a generated refinement batch, but reused across batches. Every design invocation starts simulation seeds at 300000, regardless of --seed; epoch offsets depend on those simulation seeds. Later batches therefore reuse random streams, and identical point/job combinations can reproduce identical simulations. Include a batch identifier in seed generation and detect duplicate (parameters, seed, epoch_offset, nrel) identities when loading. emulator_design.py:105–108

  5. Medium: the noise model has unquantified uncertainty and a non-identical-replicate assumption.

  6. Original runs use endpoint-inclusive deterministic epoch grids; new runs use randomly shifted grids with different spacing. Their equal means and variances are an assumption, not an established consequence of different seeds. training_set.py:182–183, grid4_common.py:58–63

  7. predict() exponentiates the fitted log-variance mean and treats the result as known. That is a plug-in estimate, not an uncertainty-integrated variance. The regression also lacks protection against invalid vjk or a singular intercept/slope fit. These are secondary while interpolation dominates, but matter when interpreting calibrated intervals. emulator.py:40–59

  8. Medium: unattended failures can look like successful completion. Workers catch failures and return them for printing; the runner does not exit unsuccessfully when jobs fail. Resume also crashes if a completed record’s spray exists but its per-star file is missing, because that file is hashed without an existence check. Require an explicit completion gate before fitting the next round. stream_batch.py:128–130, stream_batch.py:147–158, stream_batch.py:178–186

Acquisition and model choice

UCB with κ = 2 is defensible for discovering better fits. It does not directly target posterior accuracy: EI also targets improvement of the maximum, whereas posterior inference needs accurate relative likelihoods across regions carrying probability mass. Posterior-focused experimental design is the closer objective. Järvenpää et al.

The raw numerical range is not itself the problem. Positive affine rescaling—including constant tempering—leaves UCB rankings unchanged when both mean and standard deviation are scaled consistently.

My pragmatic choice would be:

  • Run 32–48 distinct points, then refit before spending the remaining budget.
  • If all 150 must run unattended, allocate roughly 100 to conservative plausible-region refinement, 30 to global discovery, and 20 to independent validation.
  • Define plausibility using an uncertainty-aware upper bound, not predicted mean alone; otherwise an inaccurate GP can exclude an undiscovered mode.
  • Keep the global GP as a scout and compare a local GP on untransformed log-likelihood differences around several promising regions. Do not introduce hard target clipping immediately before this run: it creates a plateau and changes the regression target.

The reported top-region RMSE of 1606 is insufficient evidence for posterior inference. At temperature \(T\), the relevant requirement is that errors in log-likelihood differences, divided by \(T\), are small. The temperature and those local difference errors have not been established here. The numerical validation results are supplied by the packet, not independently reproduced. [review packet:2017–2025]

1. Verified versus assumed

Verified by reading:

  • I found no sign or degrees-of-freedom error in the digamma/trigamma correction, nor a missing square in normalized GP noise. The mean fit receives s2/r and divides by ysd², consistent with scikit-learn’s variance-valued alpha. emulator.py:40–50, emulator.py:68–74, scikit-learn documentation
  • Keeping mu unchanged during fixed-kernel believer updates is mathematically appropriate when fantasy observations equal their conditional means. The questionable approximation is assigning every fantasy the median training-mean noise rather than anticipated single-run noise. emulator_design.py:88–95
  • The coordinate formulas match the training design, including the corotation-dependent size map. However, checkmap only prints discrepancies for 40 points; it neither asserts agreement nor runs automatically before design generation. emulator_design.py:31–38, training_set.py:86–99, emulator_design.py:127–130
  • Emulator tests cover a smooth toy’s average noise recovery and broad coverage bounds. They do not exercise batch selection or ingestion. The jackknife bias test uses i.i.d. toy particles, rather than randomized systematic epoch grids. test_emulator.py:8–41, test_score_bias.py:17–44

Assumed: approximately Gaussian, independent simulation errors; negligible residual jackknife bias near the optimum; interchangeable old/new epoch-grid distributions; and the packet’s numerical diagnostics. I could not run tests because the available Python environments lack the required scientific packages and pytest. Nothing was modified.

2. Strongest argument against my answer

Given interpolation errors much larger than simulation noise, further global exploration may deliver more benefit than changing acquisition or fitting a local model now. Restricting attention prematurely could miss a separate mode. If the actual 150-point selection contains no duplicates and tempering is sufficiently strong, the proposed UCB round could be a productive discovery experiment. My objections are strongest against treating its output as a validated posterior surrogate.

3. What I would check to be sure

  • Actual selected coordinates: uniqueness, separation, and distribution across plausible regions.
  • Strictly held-out top-region bias, coverage, ranking, and log-likelihood-difference errors at the intended temperature.
  • Randomized-grid replicate scatter and residual particle-number bias at the best observed and predicted points.
  • Loader rejection of duplicate runs, incompatible manifests, and inconsistent grouping keys.
  • Failure/resume tests, plus a real eight-worker smoke test for wall time, peak memory, disk use, and numerical thread counts.
  • Complete running replicates before editing their hashed sources: workers reject source changes, and resume rejects a changed manifest. stream_batch.py:86–88, stream_batch.py:133–141

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
“Orbit, not projection” is too broad for the total likelihood, but supported for the reported knee track change. The V⊙,y-only control changes the cluster’s Galactocentric initial velocity, while leaving the solar position parameters fixed; the packet reports a +620 dφ₂ score change in the knee. Since the sky coordinates are calculated from particle positions, that change must come through the changed initial condition and resulting particle positions, not a direct velocity projection effect. The code converts the cluster observables to an initial condition using frame, then projects particles using proj_frame (grid4_common.py:46–51; frames.py:31–39, 48–56). The reported control and score are in the packet (packet:2021–2029).

That does not establish that the whole I/I likelihood gain is an orbit effect. The consistent I/I run gains 841 over B/B, but the crossed runs score 345 and 3,011 below B/B; switching IC frame at Ibata projection changes the score by 3,852, while switching it at Baumgardt projection changes it by −345 (packet:2017–2028). Those are large interactions. Also, the mixed-frame runs are diagnostic controls, not self-consistent observer frames: they start the cluster in one frame and convert the debris using another. So the evidence supports an IC-driven knee-track improvement plus a substantial projection/IC interaction, not a clean decomposition of the total score.

One premise needs qualification: dφ₂ and φ₁ are computed from sky positions, but those positions are outcomes of the orbit integration. A V⊙ change can therefore alter dφ₂ through the initial velocity and subsequent trajectory even though it does not directly change the sky-coordinate transformation for fixed positions. The fixed chord frame is applied to the resulting model \(l,b\) (grid4_common.py:17–18, 54–56; path.py:67–77).

docs.title: Physical causes and next experiment
docs.text:
Ranked for this case:

  1. Solar-frame / present-day phase-space conversion. This is the only tested change here that directly shifts the inferred present-day Galactocentric velocity by the reported amount. The packet’s V⊙,y control changes that velocity and nearly reproduces the I/I total score (packet:2021–2037). The frame definitions differ in V⊙,y, R₀, and z⊙ (frames.py:16–18). The V⊙,y control is therefore strong evidence that the orbit response matters, but it does not establish that the adopted V⊙ value is physically preferable.

  2. Inner force profile and bar forcing. These can change the integrated path, especially for an orbit passing through the bar region, but they cannot change the cluster’s present-day Galactocentric velocity while its heliocentric observables and frame are fixed. The packet reports the profile-shape control as worse at fixed circular speed and describes a pericentre near 1 kpc (packet:2033–2037, 2045–2047). A halo-only normalization test is useful, but \(v_c(R₀)\) alone is a weak label for the force along a 1–7 kpc orbit.
