  3. Distance. Distance changes the tangential velocity inferred from proper motion, but the stated 5.43 ± 0.05 kpc prior is too narrow to plausibly supply a 15–20 km/s change by itself. The current W comparison instead uses 5.6 kpc (packet:2014–2015, 2033–2037); the code passes that distance explicitly into the IC conversion (grid4_common.py:40, 48). Recheck the preferred frame at 5.38, 5.43, and 5.48 kpc.

  4. LMC-induced reflex or acceleration. Published reflex signals reach tens of km/s in the distant halo, but are strongest for distant tracers with long dynamical times; they do not imply a 15–20 km/s differential correction for an object confined to the inner few kpc. Treat this as a later model extension, not the first explanation (Petersen & Peñarrubia 2020; Chandra et al. 2024).

The proposed keep_vc=False sweep is not currently implemented by that option. In axisymmetric_variant, keep_vc=False leaves the halo multiplier at c = 1; only keep_vc=True computes a normalization (mw_variants.py:37–47). Add an explicit halo normalization or target-\(v_c\) parameter. For each target, normalize the axisymmetric potential using the baryon and unit-halo force contributions; record the resulting \(v_c\) and enclosed mass at radii relevant to the orbit.

I would run the halo-only diagnostic at the existing baseline and at 220, 225, 235, and 240 km/s, with three independent seeds per point: 15 sprays, about 12.5 minutes at 50 seconds each. Keep the Baumgardt IC/projection, distance, PMs, and W bar parameters fixed. Use 215 and 245 only as stress tests if the first sweep has a trend. The packet’s ±36 lnL noise and its single seed make a one-run difference inadequate; require the trend to recur across seeds and exceed that scale before refining. Hold Ωb fixed for this first isolation; if the potential scan produces a credible shift, rescan Ωb around the best point using the same grid for baseline and modified potentials (packet:2039–2047).

Also run a whole-potential normalization as a separate controlled diagnostic if the aim is specifically to test the packet’s energy-scaling estimate. That preserves the radial shape and bar-to-axisymmetric force ratio while changing the absolute mass scale. The halo-only sweep instead keeps the baryonic bar term fixed in absolute strength and changes its fraction of the total force. The code defines bar amplitude as a multiplier on the difference between barred and axisymmetrized baryonic potentials, added to the selected axisymmetric potential (restricted.py:71–84). Report the bar-force fraction for each halo model; don’t silently interpret fixed bar_amp as fixed relative bar strength. The whole-potential scaling is not exposed by the current make_spray/host_potential interfaces (grid4_common.py:40–47; restricted.py:40–55).

docs.title: Literature bounds
docs.text:
A reasonable first-pass local range is roughly 225–235 km/s, with wider points used as diagnostics rather than plausible preferred models. Eilers et al. report \(v_c(R_0)=229.0\) km/s, with 2–5% systematic uncertainty, and exclude the inner 5 kpc because of bar-driven non-axisymmetry (arXiv:1810.09466). McMillan’s mass models give \(232.8\pm3.0\) km/s under the main assumptions, while a weakened \(R_0\) prior gives \(226.8\pm4.2\) km/s (arXiv:1608.00971). Thus 220 is a useful stress/comparison point, but these results do not support treating 215–245 as an unconstrained plausible interval.

For the inner Galaxy, Portail et al. find \(1.84\pm0.07\times10^{10}M_\odot\) in a specified bulge/bar volume of approximately \(2.2\times1.4\times1.2\) kpc, with model-dependent dark-matter fractions; their inferred bar pattern speed is \(39\pm3.5\) km/s/kpc (arXiv:1608.07954). This constrains the central mass budget, but it is not a spherical enclosed-mass constraint at every point on ω Cen’s orbit. The uncertainties and geometry matter.

docs.title: Code audit
docs.text:
• Frame split: make_spray correctly uses separate IC and projection frames; proj_frame or frame means an omitted projection frame falls back to the IC frame (grid4_common.py:40–51). The frame round-trip tests exist, but check PMs, radial velocity, and distance—not sky position or crossed-frame behavior (test_frames_roundtrip.py:6–11).
  • frame_obs_split.py: it reads and executes d1_segments.py up to the literal "\nS = {}" marker (frame_obs_split.py:8–9). This currently avoids the later top-level model loop and file writes (d1_segments.py:45–69), but it is brittle: moving or removing the marker could execute the expensive script. Put single_scores in an import-safe shared module.
  • keep_vc=False: it produces the default halo normalization, not a requested sweep point; the existing test checks default-potential reproduction, not variable halo normalization (mw_variants.py:37–47; test_mw_variants.py:10–14).

docs.title: Verified, assumed, and counterargument
docs.text:
Verified by reading code: the IC and projection frames are distinct inputs; the IC conversion uses the selected frame; the sky observables are generated from particle positions; keep_vc=False fixes the halo multiplier to 1; and the frame-split script executes source text up to a marker. The likelihoods, physical velocities, noise estimate, and orbit extrema above are reported in the packet, not independently recomputed (packet:2014–2049).

Assumptions: the reported scores use comparable inputs and scoring settings; the ±36 figure reasonably represents seed noise; and the literature mass-model constraints are applicable as broad priors to this Hunter+2024 host.

Strongest argument against my assessment: the V⊙,y-only run nearly reproduces I/I’s total score, and its knee dφ₂ gain cannot come from directly projecting fixed particle positions. That makes an IC/orbit explanation compelling. But the factorial’s large interaction shows the total score still depends strongly on how that altered orbit is projected and scored.

To be sure: verify the packet scores from the saved sprays, add repeated seeds for the potential sweep, compute \(v_c\) and enclosed mass along the orbit for each model, and test the Ωb response at any promising mass normalization.

docs.title: Codex likelihood calibration 2026 10 09
docs.text: The premise needs one correction: the score is computed for each star conditional on its observed \(u\), but the bootstrap does not hold those \(u\) positions fixed. It resamples fixed-width spatial blocks, changing the resampled star count when blocks contain different numbers of members. That matters because the conditional score deliberately omits density along \(u\) (score.py:231–245, bootstrap_grid4.py:30–40).

docs.title: Q1. Block bootstrap
docs.text:
The block bootstrap is a useful sensitivity analysis, but these results do not establish a calibrated standard error. The reported uncertainty rises across the tested block widths, while the score-difference autocorrelation remains substantial at the longest tested lag; the 4-degree resample has only nine blocks. The script tests five fixed widths and does not select one from a defensible criterion (bootstrap_grid4.py:22–24, bootstrap_grid4.py:30–48). Standard block-bootstrap inference depends on block length; automatic selectors target a specified statistic and dependence setting, not a universal “correct” block width (Bühlmann & Künsch).

I would not choose one width for the paper from this scan. Keep the untempered score and report the observed score difference, alongside the 1–4-degree sensitivity range, explicitly labeled as resampling sensitivity rather than a calibrated error bar. For inferential uncertainty, use mock calibration as the primary method. As a secondary estimate, form segment-level score and score-gradient vectors and estimate their long-run covariance; a Godambe/sandwich adjustment is relevant when the working likelihood treats dependent contributions as independent (composite-likelihood overview). It will still need mock coverage checks, and the current grid’s discrete argmax makes local curvature estimates fragile.

Miller–Dunson coarsening and generalized-Bayes learning rates are possible frameworks for tempered inference, but they require a calibration target; choosing \(N/N_{\rm eff}\) from this diagnostic would be an ad hoc rule, not a consequence of the code or these results. Coarsened posteriors can approximate fractional likelihoods and provide a calibration procedure, but that does not make an arbitrary power justified here (Miller & Dunson). A stream-segment score is useful for diagnosing where models differ, but normalizing each segment’s contribution would change the target score, not merely its uncertainty; the current code sums per-star log scores (score.py:273–275).

There is also a bootstrap design issue to fix before presenting it as inferential: the script resamples as many blocks as observed, giving each block equal draw probability regardless of its member count, then sums all its stars. The contrast is between the two models selected on the original data, and those models are held fixed in each replicate (bootstrap_grid4.py:17–20, bootstrap_grid4.py:35–45). So its reported \(P(\Delta\ln L\le0)\) is not a calibrated probability that the 20-degree model is better after refitting or reselecting.

docs.title: Q2. Spray-seed noise
docs.text:
The seed check is a useful start, but it does not isolate particle-number Monte Carlo error. It compares two parameter combinations, uses five seeds at 8,000 release epochs but only three at 32,000, and the release times are newly spaced linspaces at each particle count (seed_test.py:11–22, grid4_common.py:23–28). Thus the reported 550-lnL increase combines particle resolution, changed release-time quadrature, and the logarithm of a finite-sample KDE. It is consistent with finite-KDE bias, but it does not prove that explanation or show the bias cancels in model differences.

For a numerical approximation to each model density, average the per-member density contributions across independent sprays before taking the logarithm, then sum the resulting per-member log scores. Also compare rankings using paired seeds across the full candidate set, and increase particles until score differences stabilize. The current seed test reports log scores per spray, not a seed-averaged density (seed_test.py:21–30).

Do not combine the supplied seed and block standard deviations by simple quadrature yet. They were not measured in a crossed design, and the seed experiment uses only two models. To separate uncertainties, evaluate the same model grid over several seeds and several mock/resampled data realizations; estimate seed, data-block, and interaction components from that crossed set. Add variances only if those components are estimated for the same contrast and the independence/additivity assumption is supported.

docs.title: Q3. Cluster–knee tension
docs.text:
The opposite regional preferences are evidence of tension with this fitted setup, but do not yet identify model misfit as the cause. The grid fixes the present-day cluster proper motions at values that differ from the catalog values in OCEN_OBS; the code already has a fit path that varies both proper motions with Gaussian priors (grid4_common.py:14–27, frames.py:9–20, fit_bar_ocen.py:26–35). Also, the grid result lies at the lowest sampled bar angle, so the grid has not tested whether the optimum continues below that edge (grid4.py:20).

A cheap sequence:

  1. Re-score the same models with per-segment contributions and multiple seeds, to establish whether the regional contrast is stable.
  2. Refit with present-day proper motions free under their measurement priors; test radial velocity only if its measurement uncertainty permits a meaningful nuisance fit. The existing optimizer varies PMs but fixes the radial velocity (fit_bar_ocen.py:27–30, fit_bar_ocen.py:56–63).
  3. Extend the angle scan below 16 degrees and profile the other grid parameters. This tests the known boundary issue before adding more model complexity.
  4. Compare the spray track with compatible tracer runs to test the release prescription. The spray uses Fardal-style randomized offsets and carries the progenitor potential along the orbit (spray.py:3–12, spray.py:42–55).
  5. Only then test bar slowdown or halo changes, one at a time, against the stable regional residual pattern.

docs.title: Q4. Dark-matter detectability
docs.text:
Calibrate the A/B/C comparison with end-to-end mocks from each model: generate mock members with the same selection and measurement process, inject plausible bar, orbit, and release-model departures, then repeat the nuisance fits and A/B/C comparison. Measure false-positive rates under A and power for B and C. Use multiple spray seeds in the mocks so particle noise is represented too.

The per-star conditional KDE can be a ranking score, but treating its sum as an ordinary independent-star likelihood is not justified by the code: it sums one log score per member and has no joint dependence model (score.py:231–245, score.py:273–275). It also deliberately conditions away the along-stream density. If DM’s detectable signature is mainly in stripping rate or density along the tail, this statistic can discard that information. Mock calibration should therefore assess the conditional statistic’s power and false positives, and a density-sensitive statistic should be considered if A/B/C differ principally in counts along the stream.

docs.title: Q5. Code weaknesses and tests
docs.text:
• score_conditional has no explicit checks for compatible array shapes, a positive-width u_window, or a valid positive PM covariance determinant before division (score.py:246–260). Add edge-case tests before using it on altered catalogues or mock inputs.
  • The background is described by finite w_box and v_box widths, but the code applies the constant background density without restricting observations to those boxes. If any scored datum lies outside a box, this is not a normalized finite-box uniform component (score.py:236–245, score.py:250–256).
  • The existing score tests cover background-only cases, cancellation of \(u\)-density, duplicating a chi bin, and a kinematic shift; they do not test v_los handling, invalid covariance/window inputs, finite background support, bootstrap coverage, or seed convergence (test_score_conditional.py:24–65).

docs.title: Verified vs assumed
docs.text:
Verified by reading: the grid fixes the PMs, the conditional score sums per-star logs, the bootstrap fixes its full-data-selected contrast, and the seed test changes release-epoch spacing with particle count. The reported uncertainties, rankings, regional contrasts, sample size and astrophysical interpretation are taken from the packet; I did not reproduce those runs.

Strongest argument against this assessment: the task may only be to compare a fixed set of candidate spray models for this one observed catalogue. For that descriptive ranking, the per-star conditional KDE and block-resampling sensitivity may be adequate, and a fully generative mock calibration could add assumptions that dominate the result.

To be sure: inspect the actual grid4_perstar inputs and their provenance; check all members against the stated background boxes; reproduce the block and seed diagnostics with fixed-\(u\) and crossed resampling designs; and compare the regional result after freeing PMs and extending the angle grid. I did not run tests or recompute the reported results.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
The profile-likelihood idea is appropriate, but the supplied results do not establish that 16° is preferred once the nuisance parameters are free. The packet reports that the angle ranking reverses with distance, and that the existing grids did not jointly vary all the relevant parameters [packet:2015–2020]. Start with paired profiles at 16° and 28°; add 20° and 24° if either profile is boundary-limited or the comparison is close.

Use the same release epochs and the same seeds at every evaluation. The spray uses deterministic release epochs and a seeded random generator for the release offsets [grid4_common.py:40–51], [spray.py:105–119]. That makes the objective reproducible for a fixed seed set and pairs the Monte Carlo noise across parameter evaluations. It does not guarantee a smooth objective: score_conditional assigns particles to 5-unit chi bins, drops bins with fewer than nmin particles, and weights retained bins equally [score.py:231–275]. As parameters move particles across bin edges or change which bins qualify, the score can change abruptly. I would use a coarse search followed by bounded, multi-start Powell or COBYQA, not rely on one Nelder–Mead run.

For a practical first pass, search each angle at lower particle count, then refine several distinct candidates at the 4× particle count. Scale nuisance coordinates by meaningful increments: Ωb by 1 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹, amplitude and bar size by 0.1, distance by 0.05 kpc, and each PM by its stated 0.027 mas yr⁻¹ uncertainty. Warm-start from the existing grid optima, but also start from a small space-filling sample and from candidates at different distance/PM values. Stop when independent starts converge to the same basin and a further local refinement changes the paired score by less than its estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. If an optimum touches a nuisance bound, expand that bound where allowed and refit. If the 16° profile is still rising toward its allowed lower edge, report it as the best allowed boundary, not an interior preference. The current grid includes 16° as its lowest tested angle [grid4.py:20–21].

Treat the distance and PM measurements as external likelihood terms if the scientific question is which angle fits while respecting those measurements. Report both the data-score profile and the profile including those terms, and label the latter a penalized profile. The packet gives the proposed measurement uncertainties [packet:2020, 2026]. Do not invent Gaussian priors for bar size or amplitude: use defensible physical bounds, and show sensitivity to them. A fit that needs distance far from its measured value is evidence of tension with the external measurement, not a reason to discard it or silently temper the score.

There is no universal ΔlnL cutoff I would trust here. The score is a conditional KDE over chi bins [score.py:231–245] and the packet reports substantial seed-to-seed variation [packet:2019]. Compare paired differences, Δ = profile(16°) − profile(28°), across seeds; estimate their uncertainty by resampling seeds and stream members in along-stream blocks. Call 28° “as good” only against a practical equivalence margin calibrated on mocks, not because a generic likelihood-ratio threshold happens to be met. Three seeds can guide the search, but are too few for a dependable seed-uncertainty estimate. More particles reduce sampling noise; they do not replace independent seeds for measuring it.

Run a small recovery check before making a preference claim. Generate mock catalogues from a 28° truth, then run the same profiling procedure with distance, PMs, size, and amplitude free; include a 16° truth as a control. The existing D2 script uses 28° and 20° truths, but its candidates fix distance and omit free PM and bar-size profiling [d2_mock_recovery.py:19–20, 55–58]. Its current setup therefore cannot answer whether a 28° truth recovers 28° under the proposed profile.

docs.title: Code issues relevant to the comparison
docs.text:
• Chi-bin membership can make optimization jagged. The score selects particles with chi > 0 and age < age_max, constructs bins in fixed-width chi intervals, discards bins below nmin, and gives each retained bin equal weight [score.py:250–275]. Track K and bin membership across evaluations; test whether the angle ranking survives modest changes to dchi and nmin.
  • The 700 Myr cut is implemented. The score applies age < age_max with a default of 700 Myr [score.py:231–253]. The age comes from fixed release epochs in this setup [grid4_common.py:47–51].
  • The observed footprint is fixed in the data loader. It selects Stream 54 within latitude and longitude cuts [spray_bar_grid2.py:24–31]. The conditional score evaluates at the observed along-stream coordinates and divides by the model’s along-stream density [score.py:238–245, 273–275]. Keep the data selection and observed u_window identical across profiles.
  • Seed pairing is present, but its variance reduction is not established for this comparison. The release perturbations use a seeded generator [spray.py:105–115]; the packet reports seed scatter from other parameter settings [packet:2019]. Estimate the paired seed-difference variance at the fitted comparison points.
  • Coverage is not optimizer validation. The inspected score tests cover background-only behavior, conditional-density behavior, bin duplication, and response to altered kinematics [test_score_conditional.py:24–65]. They do not test nuisance profiling, edge handling, or mock recovery after reoptimization.

docs.title: Verified and assumed
docs.text:
Verified by reading the code: the grid fixes PMs and bar size in the cited runs [grid4.py:20–21], [sun_dist_bar_grids.py:18–22]; spray offsets are seeded [spray.py:105–115]; the score has parameter-sensitive chi-bin selection [score.py:250–275]; and the existing unit tests do not cover the proposed profiler [test_score_conditional.py:24–65].

Assumed: the packet’s reported score rankings, runtimes, catalogue uncertainties, and distance sensitivity are accurate; I did not independently rerun the grids or inspect their result files.

docs.title: Strongest argument against this recommendation
docs.text: The score may be too misspecified for nuisance profiling to answer a physically meaningful angle question: it uses fixed KDE bandwidths and equal weights for retained chi bins [score.py:231–245]. Optimizing several nuisance parameters can exploit those choices. A stable profile peak would then be a property of this scoring procedure, not strong evidence about the Galaxy’s bar angle. Mock recovery under the same score helps measure that failure, but cannot validate the score’s realism by itself.

docs.title: What I would check to be sure
docs.text:
• Recompute paired seed differences at the fitted points and verify the optima with independent seeds.
  • Check local profiles and nuisance-bound sensitivity, especially distance and PMs.
  • Measure sensitivity to chi-bin phase/width, nmin, particle count, and age cut.
  • Run free-nuisance 28° truth recovery before interpreting angle preference.
  • Check the exact data selection, fitted bar-size definition, and physical bounds used in the run. I did not run tests or modify files.

docs.title: Codex review: direct per-angle profile by optimisation on sprays (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only.

Proceed with direct profiles, but reject the premise that fixed seed and epoch offset make score differences “nearly noise-free.” They preserve random draws; they do not remove discontinuities or simulation error.

  1. Validate CRN before committing the budget. At fixed particle count, the epoch grid and age selection stay fixed as these parameters change; escape draws retain their identity. Chi-bin membership still changes discontinuously, and cutoff queries introduce additional boundaries. Thus determinism is plausible; smoothness and useful variance reduction remain unverified. Test paired parameter perturbations across several seed/offset pairs. (grid4_common.py:58–69, spray.py:55–61, spray.py:134–141, score.py:299–312, score.py:379–402)

  2. Use bounded, scaled Nelder–Mead as the first baseline. Start from two distinct nuisance-parameter locations, share CRN across both, and transfer successful solutions between neighbouring angles. Permit a third start when independent checks disagree. With 60–100 evaluations, CMA-ES at population ten gets only 6–10 generations; I would not expect a reliable eight-dimensional profile from that budget. Treat this as an empirical optimiser choice, not a convergence guarantee. Preserve the existing parameter transformation: physical bar size depends on other coordinates. (emulator_design.py:33–40)

  3. Stop using the global GP to determine the reported profile. One checked prediction is −21915, while its measured score is −23784—already enough to reject that prediction locally. A local GP may propose candidates, but require measured improvements before trusting it. Nearby off-angle runs are starting-point information, not observations of the fixed-angle objective. (emax3_0.json:15–16,49)

  4. Budget adaptively. A reasonable 400-spray allocation is approximately 20 diagnostics, 280 at 128k for search, 60 at 256k for promotion/restarts, and 40 final checks. Use 128k only after checking that candidate rankings survive promotion. Stop on exhausted budget or small search scale plus failure to improve on independent seeds; label unresolved angles unconverged. The proposed 5–6 hours excludes substantial validation work: a recorded 256k spray takes about 15 minutes. Keep fidelity explicit—the current observation loader discards nrel, seed and offset. (w3_038.json:20,51, search_wave.py:40–55)

  5. Separate three uncertainties. Report simulation standard error from independent seed/offset replicates; use paired differences when comparing angles. Report restart disagreement and further-search gains separately as unresolved optimisation error—not a symmetric confidence interval. Estimate statistical angle uncertainty from repeated mock catalogues and refitting. var_jk uses particle deletion with the catalogue fixed, so it cannot supply catalogue uncertainty or missed-basin error. (score.py:377,418–422)

Verified versus assumed

I verified the mechanisms above and inspected all three waves and the check runs. Tests cover cutoff accuracy and jackknife equivalence; I did not run them. They do not establish optimiser convergence or profile coverage. (test_score_cutoff.py:29–67)

The optimiser choice, allocation and stopping thresholds are recommendations. The −22174 benchmark remains an assumption: the plotting script hard-codes it. Acceptance at 27.5° against a 27° benchmark confounds optimisation error with angle displacement; include an exact-27° control and repeated independent truth evaluations. (plot_search_T2.py:20, mock_data.py:34)

Strongest argument against this answer

Two local searches may repeatedly miss a narrow, curved basin. Direct evaluation removes surrogate prediction error; it does not establish that the nuisance maximum was found. Four hundred sprays may therefore produce a precise-looking underestimate of the profile.

Checks needed to be sure

  • Paired CRN variance and step-size scans; repeatability under the intended worker configuration.
  • 128k/256k ranking agreement and residual bias at finalists.
  • Exact-27° recovery, additional starts, and finer angle sampling.
  • Coverage on untouched catalogues with new generating sprays.
  • Before reusing batches, verify score settings and simulation identities: the search loader checks catalogue identity but does not validate each run’s fidelity or manifest against the batch. (search_wave.py:40–55)

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
• Use stream-aligned coordinates for reporting, but let the track curve. A great-circle frame is a useful coordinate system and zero-point, not a physical assumption that the stream follows one great circle. For these data, fit a robust, curved, two-dimensional path and estimate proper motion, distance, radial velocity, and width as functions of position along it.
  • Treat the published membership lists as selected data. STREAMFINDER scores stars against orbit templates, so fitting the same list’s mean track can inherit template bias. Use the lists for an initial measurement, then compare against an independently selected Gaia sample or quantify the bias with injection and recovery through STREAMFINDER.
  • Start the model search with sprays, then validate against the existing tracer runs. Sprays can integrate debris in a rotating, time-dependent bar potential and are suitable for broad parameter exploration. Their escape prescription is approximate; progenitor spin and the substantial cluster mass make a targeted higher-fidelity comparison important. The newer Chen et al. spray paper reports about 10% morphology and velocity accuracy against its N-body tests, not a guarantee for this particular orbit.
  • Fit the bar and host before testing cluster dark matter. First find the acceptable bar and host region while marginalizing over ω Cen’s present-day phase space. Then compare the no-DM, moderate-DM, and 5×-DM-inside-200-pc cases by refitting nuisance parameters under each hypothesis and testing recovery on mock data.
  • The stream data supplied here favor a bar, but do not yet identify a unique bar. The stated proper-motion gradient agreement at \(\Omega_b=33\) and partial sky-track bend are encouraging. A single short, selected stream segment is unlikely to separate bar pattern speed, bar strength, host structure, and progenitor phase space without external priors and independent track validation.

docs.title: A. Measuring the observed track
docs.text:
Standard approaches. A stream-aligned great-circle rotation, such as the GD-1 \((\phi_1,\phi_2)\) frame, is a convenient way to define along- and cross-stream coordinates. It works well for organizing data and fitting a nearly planar stream, but it does not require the stream to be planar. The GD-1 work established this style of coordinate system and showed how a stream’s phase-space map can be fit; the Orphan–Chenab analysis later demonstrates why a long stream’s pole can drift substantially. Koposov, Rix & Hogg 2010, ApJ; arXiv:0907.1085, DOI:10.1088/0004-637X/712/1/260 Koposov et al. 2019, MNRAS; arXiv:1812.08192, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stz457

For a local, clean stream segment, a low-order polynomial or spline in \(\phi_2(\phi_1)\) is a practical track model. Erkal et al.’s Pal 5 analysis jointly modeled a spline track, width, density, and background. The S⁵ Orphan–Chenab analysis reconstructed sky track, proper motion, radial velocity, distance, and density with spline models. Ferguson et al.’s Jet analysis likewise used natural splines for track, width, and intensity. These methods provide interpretable tracks and uncertainties, but standard one-dimensional splines assume the stream is a function of the chosen along-stream coordinate. Erkal, Koposov & Belokurov 2017, MNRAS; arXiv:1609.01282, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stw2357 Koposov et al. 2023, MNRAS; arXiv:2211.04495, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stad551 Ferguson et al. 2021, ApJ; arXiv:2104.11755, DOI:10.3847/1538-4357/ac0e2a

For a strongly curved path, a method that reconstructs the path without forcing \(\phi_2\) to be a single-valued function of \(\phi_1\) is safer. Starkman et al.’s TrackStream uses self-organizing maps and Kalman filtering; the authors report that it handles sparse data and phase-wrapped paths while propagating path uncertainty. A full probabilistic alternative is the mixture-density approach of Starkman et al., which jointly estimates track, width, density, kinematics, membership, and background. Starkman et al. 2023, MNRAS; arXiv:2212.00949, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stad100 Starkman et al. 2023, ApJ; arXiv:2311.16960, DOI:10.3847/1538-4357/ad00f0

What STREAMFINDER contributes and what it does not. The DR3 atlas paper constructs a separate great-circle frame for each stream, with coordinates oriented along the stream velocity; for known globular-cluster progenitors it anchors the frame on the cluster. This is a useful convention for comparing streams and models. The same paper says that sky-position errors are negligible for its great-circle fitting, an assumption that is usually safe for Gaia positions but says nothing about uncertain membership or selection. Ibata et al. 2024, “Charting the Galactic Acceleration Field II,” peer-reviewed published version; arXiv:2311.17202 Cambridge repository record

STREAMFINDER evaluates stars against trial-orbit templates and a stream “hypertube,” using astrometric, kinematic, and population information. Consequently, a member list selected this way is not a random sample of the stream’s true phase-space distribution. The selection can favor stars that lie near the templates used in the search. Malhan & Ibata 2018, “STREAMFINDER—I,” MNRAS; DOI:10.1093/mnras/sty1036 The DR3 atlas paper’s reported streams and stellar masses also depend on the extent of the identified stream, its assumed stellar population, and a completeness assumption; it explicitly describes some mass estimates as rough. Ibata et al. 2024; arXiv:2311.17202

Practical recommendation for streams 54 and 55.

  1. Set a fixed spherical coordinate frame for each candidate, anchored on ω Cen and with the initial along-stream axis chosen from the observed arm. Keep that frame fixed for both data and all models. Use it to label \(\phi_1,\phi_2\), not to impose a great-circle shape.
  2. Measure a curved sky path with a robust spline or TrackStream-like path estimator. Fit robust location and intrinsic scatter in \(\phi_2\), both proper-motion components, distance, and radial velocity as functions of path length or a locally monotonic \(\phi_1\). Fit the distance modulus offset track as well as any available absolute-distance estimates, with a separate zero-point nuisance term.
  3. Use bins or adaptive windows large enough to yield stable estimates. Within each, use a contamination-resistant location estimate or a stream/background mixture model, and carry through Gaia’s per-star astrometric covariance. Estimate uncertainty by resampling spatial blocks or using a fitted covariance model; ordinary bootstrap resampling of individual stars would understate errors if nearby selected members have correlated selection.
  4. Report the fitted path, width, and kinematic tracks with a covariance matrix or posterior samples. Keep radial-velocity points at their actual locations rather than smoothing them into falsely precise bins. The user-supplied member counts and velocity counts are analysis inputs here; they are not independently verified by the cited papers.
  5. Do not use member counts or density as a dynamical likelihood initially. Unknown STREAMFINDER completeness, crowding, magnitude limits, and foreground contamination make density harder to interpret than the centroid track. A later density analysis requires a selection model.

To assess template bias, repeat the track measurement using a Gaia parent sample selected independently of STREAMFINDER—for example, a broad sky/colour/magnitude region followed by a cross-validated mixture or chemical/kinematic selection. If this cannot be assembled immediately, treat the STREAMFINDER track as a potentially biased summary: add a systematic track-error floor and exclude the most template-sensitive portion from the primary fit. The strongest check is injection and recovery: pass synthetic stream stars through the original selection and measure how much the recovered track shifts. Gaia subset selection can itself have strong spatial, magnitude, and colour dependence; this is documented for Gaia DR3 subsets generally. Castro-Ginard et al. 2023, “Estimating the selection function of Gaia DR3 sub-samples”; arXiv:2303.17738

Keep streams 54 and 55 separate at first. The DR3 atlas labels #54 Fimbulthul and #55 Fimbulthul-S; the atlas highlights the nearby trailing ω Cen arm. Separately, recent spectroscopy reports that stream #55 is in the same action–energy region as Fimbulthul. That is evidence for a relationship, not proof that the two observed sequences are one continuous arm or were selected without overlap. Fit each separately, check for duplicate Gaia sources, and then test a joint model with a shared host and progenitor but separate membership/selection components. Ibata et al. 2024; arXiv:2311.17202 “Disruption of a giant,” MNRAS (2026)

docs.title: B. Generating model tracks
docs.text:
Fast options.

  • Orbit-only models are useful for initial exploration, but an orbit is not a stream. Stream–orbit offsets matter, especially for a massive, disrupting progenitor and for the knee.
  • Particle spray / Lagrange-point stripping releases tracer particles near the progenitor’s tidal boundary and integrates them in the host potential. Fardal et al. calibrated an ejection prescription against N-body models; Gibbons et al. developed a related particle-release method. These methods are fast and naturally include subsequent perturbations to already released particles. Their weaknesses are approximate escape physics, simplified mass loss, and errors near the progenitor or for complicated stripping histories. Fardal, Huang & Weinberg 2015, MNRAS; arXiv:1410.1861, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stv1198 Gibbons, Belokurov & Evans 2014, MNRAS; arXiv:1406.2243, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stu692
  • Improved spray. Chen et al. (2024 preprint) calibrate release distributions against cluster N-body runs and report roughly 10% accuracy in stream morphology and velocities in their tests. Their implementation is reported for AGAMA, gala, galax, and galpy. This is a promising first choice, but its published accuracy is not a validated error budget for ω Cen on this orbit, with this bar and this internal rotation. Chen et al. 2024, preprint; arXiv:2408.01496
  • Restricted N-body / tracer integrations are the natural middle ground when the cluster potential is prescribed: integrate a cluster model or sampled tracers in the external potential, with whatever cluster–tracer force treatment the existing runs use. The supplied local timing—3.4 minutes for axisymmetric and 6.5 minutes for barred models on eight threads—is especially valuable: it provides a measured, higher-fidelity validation tier.
  • Live direct N-body is the reference for internal cluster dynamics, mass loss, and rotation, but is expensive for broad bar-parameter fitting. Reserve it for a small number of calibration models if the fixed-potential tracer treatment cannot capture the relevant escape physics.

Time-dependent bar and progenitor spin. A spray is mathematically compatible with a time-dependent host: integrate the progenitor orbit in the rotating potential, release particles at their modeled escape times, then integrate each released particle in that same time-dependent potential. gala documents mock-stream generation with rotating/non-static reference frames; AGAMA’s Hunter et al. example constructs an explicitly rotating bar potential with a specified present-day phase and pattern speed. These establish implementation feasibility, not accuracy of a particular spray prescription under bar-driven chaotic or strongly varying tides. gala mock-stream documentation AGAMA Hunter+2024 example

Internal rotation deserves explicit attention here. The original Fimbulthul N-body interpretation used an ω Cen model with internal rotation; a recent Pal 5 discussion also summarizes that the ω Cen–Fimbulthul models require some level of progenitor rotation. A standard isotropic spray does not automatically encode spin-dependent escape. Treat progenitor spin direction and amplitude as an uncertainty in calibration runs, or use a spin-aware release model validated against rotating-cluster N-body simulations. Do not let an uncalibrated spray spin prescription decide the dark-matter result. Ibata et al. 2019, Nature Astronomy; arXiv:1902.09544, DOI:10.1038/s41550-019-0751-x “Forward and back: kinematics of the Palomar 5 tidal tails,” MNRAS (2022)

Cost. There is no defensible universal “seconds per model” from the papers: it depends on particle count, integrator, hardware, bar representation, and code. For campaign planning, benchmark a small grid of spray models first, then use the measured median and 90th-percentile runtime. The supplied tracer timings imply that 100 such runs would cost about 5–11 hours on the same eight-thread setup, before analysis overhead; that makes tracer runs suitable for validation and targeted refinement, not a large sampler. A spray search can be budgeted by wall-clock after the benchmark rather than assumed free.

Build model summaries identically to data. Transform model particles to the same heliocentric frame and stream coordinates; apply identical magnitude/colour cuts, measurement errors, distance-modulus treatment, velocity availability, and bin/window locations. For each data bin, measure model medians/means and intrinsic scatter with the same robust estimator used on the observations. Convolve model observables with observational covariance before evaluating the fit. Apply either a Gaia completeness model and contamination model or an approximate STREAMFINDER selection function; otherwise omit density terms. If STREAMFINDER injection/recovery becomes available, apply the same recovery process to mocks and data.

docs.title: C. Fitting strategy and parameter identifiability
docs.text:
Objective. A practical likelihood is a multivariate Gaussian (or Student-t / mixture) likelihood for the track observables in each bin:

\[ \log L = -\frac12 \sum_j (\mathbf y_j-\mathbf m_j)^\mathsf{T} \left(\mathbf C_{\mathrm{obs},j}+\mathbf C_{\mathrm{model},j}+\mathbf C_{\mathrm{sys},j}\right)^{-1} (\mathbf y_j-\mathbf m_j) -\frac12\sum_j \log |\mathbf C_j|. \]

Here \(\mathbf y_j\) contains sky position, proper motion, and available distance and radial velocity; \(\mathbf m_j\) is the matched model summary. Include intrinsic model scatter, measurement covariance, and a systematic floor for selection and track-estimation uncertainty. Avoid treating every selected star as an independent likelihood contribution when the actual objective is a smooth track. Erkal et al.’s Orphan analysis adds observational and simulated-stream variances in a per-star likelihood; the S⁵ Orphan–Chenab work fits a six-dimensional track with spline summaries and stripping models. Erkal et al. 2019, MNRAS; arXiv:1812.08192, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stz1371 Koposov et al. 2023; arXiv:2211.04495

Fit the knee as part of the curved track, not as an isolated angle measurement. A good secondary diagnostic is its curvature or a predeclared local displacement from a smooth reference track, evaluated over a fixed \(\phi_1\) interval. This makes it harder for flexible splines to erase the feature or for model binning to move it.

Parameters and priors.

  • Bar: pattern speed \(\Omega_b\), present-day angle, amplitude or mass normalization, and at most one bar-size/shape parameter. Start with the supplied Hunter et al. potential family. Use external information as a prior or sensitivity range, not as an absolute truth: published pattern-speed estimates differ substantially by method. For example, Portail et al.’s made-to-measure model reports \(39.0\pm3.5\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}\,kpc^{-1}}\), while Clarke & Gerhard report \(33.29\pm1.81\) from a different bulge proper-motion comparison. Portail et al. 2017, MNRAS; arXiv:1608.07954, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stw2819 Clarke & Gerhard 2022, MNRAS; arXiv:2107.10875, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stab3451
  • Host: initially fix or tightly regularize the disk and halo to the Hunter model; then vary a small number of parameters such as halo normalization/flattening or disk mass/scale. The DR3 atlas supplies one useful axisymmetric-stream prior, but it is not a barred-stream fit and should not be imported as a precise constraint on this orbit. Ibata et al. 2024; arXiv:2311.17202
  • Progenitor: use Gaussian priors for ω Cen’s current six-dimensional phase-space coordinates based on the adopted catalogue and Gaia astrometry, including their covariances. Keep these as nuisance parameters: even a modest shift can alter where the released debris falls on the sky.
  • Release physics: stream age / release-time range, progenitor mass and scale, and spin parameters (or a calibrated fixed spin prescription). The supplied estimate that material at \(b>30^\circ\) was released 300–600 Myr ago is a prior from the stated local analysis, not an independently verified literature constraint.

Pattern speed and present-day angle both influence bar phase at past stripping times; bar strength trades off against the host’s non-axisymmetric force and progenitor phase space. Halo flattening, disk mass, and bar amplitude can all shift the track. Distance shifts and solar-reflex corrections affect proper-motion interpretation; sparse radial velocities limit how much they can break degeneracies. The knee plus the observed proper-motion gradient can constrain different aspects of the time-dependent perturbation, but only if the same track is measured without template imprint.

Optimizer and sampling. Use a coarse grid or Latin-hypercube / CMA-ES search to find viable basins; refine with a derivative-free local optimizer if sprays introduce Monte Carlo noise. Then sample the posterior with an ensemble MCMC or nested sampler using fixed random seeds/common random numbers where possible, to reduce simulation noise in parameter differences. An emulator is worthwhile only after the parameter-to-summary map is smooth enough and its prediction error is checked on withheld models. At seconds-to-minutes per model, fitting four bar parameters plus many host and progenitor parameters with brute-force MCMC is a poor starting point.

docs.title: D. Staged campaign and dark-matter test
docs.text:
Stage Work and decision point Planning budget 0. Freeze observables Build separate data summaries for #54 and #55 in one fixed frame; inspect overlaps and duplicate sources; quantify track covariance, membership contamination, CMD-shift uncertainty, and velocity-bin support. Produce an independent Gaia-selected comparison or mark the track systematics as provisional. Proceed to dynamics only if the knee persists under reasonable track estimators and membership cuts. Data-analysis effort; no model grid. 1. Spray benchmark and control Benchmark runtime and numerical stability for a small set of sprays in axisymmetric and barred Hunter potentials. Confirm the present-day progenitor prior and release-time coverage. Compare simple orbit-only, baseline spray, and current tracer outputs at a few fixed parameter points. About 10–20 models; replace with measured cost after benchmark. 2. Bar/host discovery fit Use a rotating-bar spray, fit #54 first, then test a joint #54/#55 fit. Fit \(\Omega_b\), angle, bar amplitude, and progenitor phase-space nuisance terms; initially regularize the axisymmetric host and hold bar shape fixed. Include the matched 6D observables, not density. Reject models that fit PMs but miss the independently measured knee/sky track. Roughly 500–2,000 spray evaluations as an initial search envelope; wall-time depends on benchmark. 3. Posterior and degeneracy checks Refine the bar fit, vary a limited host parameter set, and assess whether bar parameters are actually identified or merely trade off with nuisance terms. Test STREAMFINDER injection/recovery or enlarge systematic errors if the bias remains unknown. Roughly 2,000–10,000 evaluations, chosen after Stage 2 shows how many parameters are needed. 4. High-fidelity validation Run the existing tracer method at representative posterior points: best fit, low/high \(\Omega_b\), and a contrasting bar phase/strength. Compare track, PM gradient, knee, widths, and debris release-time distribution against sprays. Include at least one rotating-progenitor calibration if feasible. About 10–30 tracer models; at the supplied timing, roughly 1–3.5 hours on eight threads. 5. Dark-matter model comparison For each of the three stipulated ω Cen DM cases, rerun/refit bar, host, phase-space, and release nuisance parameters under identical priors and selection treatment. Compute evidence or a likelihood-ratio statistic and posterior predictive differences. Use mocks from each case to measure false-positive rate and power. First use sprays for all three cases; validate a small number of each with tracer runs. Mock count depends on measured spray cost and the precision required.

The specific detectability test: compare three discrete hypotheses—no DM, moderate DM, and 5× DM inside 200 pc—using the same data likelihood, priors, and selection treatment. Marginalize over bar, host, ω Cen’s present phase space, and release/spin parameters separately under each hypothesis. Report posterior model probabilities or Bayes factors, plus a posterior-predictive separation in the joint track/PM/distance/velocity summaries.

Call the DM effect measurable only if (a) the preferred DM hypothesis remains favored after nuisance refitting and after plausible track-selection systematics are included, and (b) blinded mock recovery distinguishes that hypothesis with calibrated false-positive rate and useful power. A practical initial bar is a Bayes factor above 100 (\(\Delta\ln Z>4.6\)) and successful recovery in mocks; this is a campaign decision threshold, not a universal scientific standard. If the streams’ widths or velocities are what carry the separation, include them only after confirming their measurement and selection models. A difference between best-fit tracks alone is not evidence of detection if the bar or progenitor nuisance parameters can absorb it.

docs.title: Disagreements, uncertainties, and open questions
docs.text:
• Stream #55’s relationship to Fimbulthul is not settled by shared action–energy location. The label “Fimbulthul-S” and spectroscopy support analyzing it as a plausible ω Cen-associated structure, but neither source establishes that its sample is an unbiased continuation of #54. Keep the fits separate until the data support a joint model.
  • Published bar pattern speeds disagree. The estimates cited above arise from different dynamical tracers and model assumptions. The stated local fit at \(\Omega_b=33\) is consistent with one published estimate and distinct from others; it should be interpreted as a stream-specific fit conditional on the host, bar model, and membership track.
  • Spray accuracy is not yet demonstrated for this exact problem. Chen et al.’s roughly 10% result comes from its simulation suite. The ω Cen orbit is massive, rotating, and passes through a barred, time-dependent field; the tracer cross-check is essential.
  • Selection uncertainty can dominate formal track errors. The STREAMFINDER membership list is useful and information-rich, but its orbit-template selection makes the track measurement partly endogenous. Without independent Gaia selection or injection/recovery, uncertainty bars from the selected members alone are too optimistic.
  • A single segment may not constrain bar slowdown. With the supplied 300–600 Myr release-time range and current stream coverage, fit a constant pattern speed first. Slowdown adds a time-history degree of freedom that is likely degenerate with bar strength, phase, and progenitor initial conditions; add it only if a constant-speed posterior fails structured residual checks and mocks show recoverability.
  • “5× DM inside 200 pc” needs an explicit density profile and time evolution. The enclosed dark mass alone does not define the tidal force at the cluster’s limiting radius or its past mass loss. Before interpreting the three hypotheses, specify how DM is spatially distributed, whether it is bound to ω Cen, and how that component evolves under stripping.
  • No published source fixes the campaign’s runtime. The supplied 3.4/6.5-minute tracer timing is a local measured result. Spray runtime should be benchmarked in the actual implementation before assigning a firm posterior-sampling budget.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
• The Galactic bar is the leading physical candidate, but it is not yet an explanation. Omega Cen’s low-pericentre orbit repeatedly enters the bar’s strong-force region, and published simulations show that a rotating bar can give neighboring debris different torques near pericentre. But the reported PM change is large: at 4.8 kpc, 90 km/s is about 4 mas/yr. The bar must produce a strongly differential kick to the distal arm, not merely change the cluster’s orbit.
  • The apparent 1 kpc displacement and 90 km/s difference are hard to reconcile if both persist over hundreds of Myr. A 90 km/s velocity difference maintained for 300 Myr corresponds to about 28 kpc of relative travel. A viable perturbation must therefore be brief, project mostly along an unobserved direction, or indicate that the measured ridge is not one continuous stream population.
  • The bar is a better match than the other named smooth perturbers. LMC reflex motion is largely common to this nearby structure; a smooth halo-shape or disc-mass change should alter the orbit coherently; spiral forcing is weaker at the knee’s estimated Galactocentric height; and a giant molecular cloud or Sagittarius encounter could matter only with a sufficiently close, favorably timed passage.
  • The published spectroscopy supports an ω Cen association near the start of the bend, but does not settle the distal knee. GALAH reported two candidate stars at \(b=33^\circ\) and \(37^\circ\), with \(v_{\rm los}=215\)–219 km/s and [Fe/H] = −1.88 and −1.53. These lie around \(l\approx-49^\circ\) to \(-51^\circ\), before the reported \(l\approx-30^\circ\) to \(-45^\circ\) knee. I found no published S⁵, APOGEE, or Gaia RVS study that independently samples the distal knee.
  • STREAMFINDER could affect the inferred track and membership, but cannot by itself manufacture the Gaia measurements. Its candidates are selected for compatibility with trial orbit templates. That makes a template-selection or population-joining artifact testable; it does not make the measured proper motions or distances artifacts automatically.

docs.title: 1. Which mechanism could make a bend this large?
docs.text:
The requested scale is substantial. Using \(v_t=4.74047\,d\,\mu\), a 90 km/s tangential difference at \(d=4.8\) kpc is \(3.95\) mas/yr. A 15° angular offset at that distance corresponds to 1.26 kpc. These are conversions from the values in the question, not independent measurements.

The location also makes the bar relevant. For a representative knee point near \(l=-38^\circ,\ b=36^\circ,\ d=4.8\) kpc and \(R_0=8.1\) kpc, the Galactocentric cylindrical radius is roughly 5.5–6 kpc and the height is about 2.8 kpc. That places the present-day knee near the commonly estimated bar corotation radius, while the cluster’s stated pericentre lies well inside it. Portail et al. measured a bar pattern speed of \(39.0\pm3.5\) km s\(^{-1}\) kpc\(^{-1}\) and a corotation radius \(6.1\pm0.5\) kpc in their model; another analysis found \(33.29\pm1.81\) km s\(^{-1}\) kpc\(^{-1}\), implying a corotation range of 6.5–7.5 kpc under its rotation-curve assumptions. These are model-dependent constraints, not a direct measurement of Omega Cen’s resonance state. (Portail et al. 2017, arXiv:1608.07954; Clarke & Gerhard 2021, arXiv:2107.10875)

A circular-orbit corotation radius is not itself proof that this eccentric, retrograde cluster is resonantly trapped. For eccentric orbits, the relevant condition involves radial and azimuthal frequencies as well as bar speed. A 2026 preprint on a different, long-term question—whether the bar could have moved Omega Cen from Gaia-Sausage–Enceladus-like phase space—finds that its proposed migration requires a very slow present-day bar, \(\Omega_b\lesssim26\) km s\(^{-1}\) kpc\(^{-1}\). That is below most current estimates. It therefore does not support a claim that Omega Cen is currently in that particular resonance. It does establish that bar-orbit coupling has been studied explicitly for Omega Cen, under assumptions about its origin and the bar’s past evolution. (Dillamore, Zhang & Belokurov 2026, preprint, arXiv:2606.12516)

Mechanism Order-of-magnitude assessment for this case Rotating bar Best candidate; potentially tens of km/s per strong pericentre passage, with a larger cumulative or differential effect possible near a suitable resonance. As a scale estimate, take a bar force fraction \(Q_b\sim0.05\)–0.15 of the total force at \(R\sim2\) kpc and \(V_c\sim200\) km/s. Then \(a_b\sim Q_bV_c^2/R\), or roughly 1–3 km/s per Myr while traversing the inner few kpc. A 10–20 Myr strong-force passage gives a gross impulse of order 10–60 km/s. This is only an order-of-magnitude bound: the difference between debris stars’ impulses depends on their positions and passage times relative to bar orientation. Several pericentric passages in 300–600 Myr make a large differential effect conceivable, but the estimate does not demonstrate a 90 km/s kick. Hattori et al. describe exactly this differential-torque mechanism for Ophiuchus; Pearson et al. find that a rotating bar can reproduce Pal 5’s asymmetry in their models. (Hattori et al. 2016, arXiv:1512.04536; Pearson, Price-Whelan & Johnston 2017, arXiv:1703.04627) Spiral arms Probably secondary. Spiral forcing can alter orbits, but the estimated knee height is nearly 3 kpc above the plane, where a thin-disc spiral perturbation is reduced. Omega Cen’s disc crossings could still matter. A few to perhaps tens of km/s is a reasonable scale for a favorable repeated interaction; a localized 90 km/s tangential change is not the default expectation. Giant molecular clouds Possible only through a close encounter. The impulse approximation gives \(\Delta v\sim2GM/(bV)\). A \(10^7\,M_\odot\) cloud at \(b=0.1\) kpc and \(V=50\) km/s gives about 17 km/s; a \(10^8\,M_\odot\) complex at that impact parameter could approach 170 km/s. Such a close massive encounter is exceptional, and the stream segment would need to pass near the cloud. This is a targeted-encounter hypothesis, not a generic effect. LMC and inner-Galaxy reflex motion Small differential effect across this nearby stream segment. For an illustrative \(10^{11}\,M_\odot\) LMC at 50 kpc, the tidal acceleration difference across 5 kpc is \(GM r/D^3\); integrated for 0.5 Gyr it gives about 9 km/s. The reflex motion measured against distant halo stars can be tens of km/s, but much of that is common-mode for the cluster and its nearby debris. The literature’s \(\sim40\) km/s inner-Galaxy reflex result is measured relative to stars at about 100 kpc, not as a 40 km/s differential kick across Fimbulthul. (Chandra et al. 2024, arXiv:2406.01676) Sagittarius Could be important if a close encounter occurred; otherwise likely subdominant. As a deliberately favorable example, a \(4\times10^{10}\,M_\odot\) perturber at \(b=20\) kpc and \(V=200\) km/s gives a total impulse near 86 km/s. Across a 5 kpc stream segment, the differential part is much smaller unless the encounter geometry is especially close. Simulations of GD-1-like streams find that recently stripped stars are generally less affected by Sagittarius than older debris, although some configurations produce strong changes. The result depends on encounter geometry and stripping age. (Dillamore et al. 2022, arXiv:2205.13547) Halo flattening or triaxiality Can change orbital-plane precession and the global track; less naturally makes a sharp, local PM jump. The STREAMFINDER DR3 atlas’s preferred halo fit has density flattening \(q_{m,h}=0.75\pm0.03\), conditional on its model and stream sample. That is evidence against assuming a spherical halo, not a direct bound on the stream’s short-term kick. A strongly non-axisymmetric halo could make the orbit more complex, but the mechanism would need to explain why the discrepant behavior appears at the distal arm while the near-cluster arm agrees. (Ibata et al. 2024, arXiv:2311.17202) Disc mass or smooth-potential errors Could shift the integrated orbit; unlikely to produce the whole local anomaly alone. Changing the disc/bulge force changes pericentre speed and precession. But a smooth axisymmetric change acts on the cluster and recently released debris together. The supplied fact that McMillan17 and DB98 models both miss the knee weakens a simple axisymmetric-potential explanation. It does not test a rotating bar or a live, time-dependent Galaxy. Omega Cen’s present-day phase-space uncertainty Unlikely to explain 90 km/s if Gaia cluster astrometry and the systemic radial velocity are used. A 1 mas/yr proper-motion shift at 5.6 kpc is about 27 km/s, so a 90 km/s shift would require roughly 3.4 mas/yr in the cluster’s input PM. That is far larger than the formal uncertainty of a well-measured cluster mean. Distance uncertainty changes the conversion and orbit, but would have to be implausibly large to supply the full mismatch. A full covariance propagation remains important because a small present-day error can accumulate into an appreciable positional error after several orbits.

The bar literature supports bar-driven stream reshaping in principle, especially for low-pericentre streams. Hattori et al. show that nearby debris stars reach pericentre at slightly different times and thus encounter a rotating bar at different orientations; their resulting energy and angular-momentum differences change stream growth. The work focuses on Ophiuchus, not Omega Cen. Pearson et al. show a bar model that can reproduce Pal 5’s leading/trailing length asymmetry and gaps. This is evidence that the mechanism can produce observable stream structure, not evidence that it produces this particular Fimbulthul PM knee. (Hattori et al. 2016, arXiv:1512.04536; Pearson et al. 2017, arXiv:1703.04627)

There is also a useful caution from newer work: simulations of the bar’s effect on old substructure find strong dispersion for some low-energy, low-inclination populations, while high-inclination streams can be less affected. That work identifies Pal 5 and Ophiuchus among streams in its bar-susceptible region; it does not establish that Fimbulthul is similarly affected. The result depends on the adopted bar model and on the orbit integrals used to classify structures. (Dillamore et al. 2025, MNRAS, DOI:10.1093/mnras/staf1264)

The displacement/velocity tension is the strongest physical objection to a simple bar-kick story. If a 90 km/s difference had persisted for 300 Myr, it would produce roughly 28 kpc of separation. So a bar explanation needs a fairly specific history: a short impulse near a recent passage, a velocity difference largely along the line of sight or stream direction rather than the sky offset, or a resonant torque that changes the present velocity while leaving a relatively modest projected separation. A forward model must demonstrate all of those together.

docs.title: 2. Literature on the bar and Omega Cen or inner-orbit streams
docs.text:
The strongest directly relevant studies are:

  • Ophiuchus: Hattori, Erkal & Sanders explain how a rotating bar can torque stream stars differently at pericentre and create unusually short or altered streams. This is peer-reviewed MNRAS work, published in 2016; it is a close dynamical analogy, not an Omega Cen-tail model. (arXiv:1512.04536; MNRAS DOI:10.1093/mnras/stw1006)
  • Pal 5: Pearson, Price-Whelan & Johnston report that a rotating-bar model can reproduce the observed length asymmetry and gaps in Pal 5. The paper appeared in Nature Astronomy in 2017. Its orbit and data differ from Fimbulthul’s. (arXiv:1703.04627)
  • Pal 5 perturbation evidence: Erkal, Koposov & Belokurov find Pal 5 density structure inconsistent with an unperturbed stream in their simulations and discuss bar and GMC explanations alongside subhaloes. Their study does not uniquely attribute the observed features to the bar. (arXiv:1609.01282; MNRAS DOI:10.1093/mnras/stw2584)
  • Omega Cen orbit in a bar: The 2026 Dillamore et al. preprint tests bar-driven migration over the long-term formation history. Its proposed resonance requires a pattern speed below typical current estimates. That is not a model of Fimbulthul’s last 300–600 Myr, and it argues against casually calling Omega Cen “in resonance” just because the pericentre lies inside the bar’s corotation radius. (arXiv:2606.12516)

The reported orbital period of about 90 Myr means 300–600 Myr of debris age covers roughly 3–7 periods, consistent with the “4–6 pericentres” estimate in the question. That creates enough repeated inner passages for a time-dependent perturbation to matter. But there is no cited published barred-potential model showing the observed Fimbulthul PM sequence or a 90 km/s differential kick.

docs.title: 3. Spectroscopy and the STREAMFINDER-selection question
docs.text:
Published spectroscopy beyond \(b=30^\circ\):

  • Ibata et al. 2019: The discovery/association paper reports high-resolution spectra for five stream stars, closely grouped in velocity and chemically consistent with Omega Cen. The paper’s [Fe/H] measurements for four usable spectra span about −1.4 to −1.8 dex, with mean uncertainty 0.11 dex. These observations supported the original association, but they predate the distal DR3 extension and do not provide a dense RV map of the newly described knee. (Ibata et al. 2019, Nature Astronomy, DOI:10.1038/s41550-019-0751-x; arXiv:1902.09544)
  • GALAH: Simpson et al. searched the known stream region at \(b>30^\circ\), selecting GALAH fields within 4° of the stream track and applying broad velocity, parallax, and PM cuts. They found two new candidate members: at \((l,b)=(311.06^\circ,37.19^\circ)\), \(v_{\rm rad}=218.5\) km/s and [Fe/H] \(=-1.53\pm0.08\); and \((308.75^\circ,32.86^\circ)\), \(v_{\rm rad}=214.8\) km/s and [Fe/H] \(=-1.88\pm0.07\). The two stars are at \(l\approx-49^\circ\) and \(-51^\circ\), so they test the section leading into the bend, not the reported \(l\approx-30^\circ\) to \(-45^\circ\) distal knee. The authors also stress that GALAH’s footprint was sparse and that the original stream candidates were generally too faint for GALAH. (Simpson et al. 2020, MNRAS 491, 3374, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stz3105; arXiv:1911.01548)
  • Omega Cen’s inner tidal extensions: A 2026 VLT/FLAMES study identifies five high-probability members in tidal extensions out to 3.2° from the cluster and finds kinematic and metallicity continuity with the cluster. It is valuable support for ongoing stripping, but those fields do not reach the distant \(b>30^\circ\) knee. (Kuzma et al. 2026, MNRAS 550, stag1147, DOI:10.1093/mnras/stag1147; arXiv:2605.23474)

I found no published S⁵, APOGEE, or Gaia RVS member analysis that samples the distal knee itself. That is not proof that no individual survey spectra exist there; it means the papers located do not establish the knee’s RV and chemical sequence independently. GALAH is the clearest published independent check along the high-latitude arm, and its two high-latitude candidates are at the pre-knee longitude.

What STREAMFINDER can and cannot explain: STREAMFINDER assigns significance to stars as members of groups along trial orbits, using positional and kinematic compatibility. A template-based selection can favor some parts of phase space, miss a complex true stream, or make a catalogued ridge look more continuous than a blind selection would. The original algorithm paper describes orbit-based selection and also warns that structures on complex orbits can be missed. (Malhan & Ibata 2018, MNRAS 477, 4063, DOI:10.1093/mnras/sty912; arXiv:1804.11338)

That does not mean the algorithm can invent the measured PMs of selected Gaia stars. The discriminating test is to inspect the underlying Gaia DR3 sources and their local phase-space distribution with no STREAMFINDER membership score or orbit prior: are there two distinct PM/RV clumps that the selected catalog stitches together, or is there a continuous sequence with a sharp but real bend? A blind chemical and spectroscopic check is especially important because the distal tail is crowded and contaminated.

The question’s Gaia XP sample—bright giants at the knee, near the cluster, and in stream 55—has modest sample sizes (16–19 per comparison group). The reported KS \(p=0.17\)–0.80 does not reject a common [M/H] distribution, but it does not establish equivalence or prove common origin. The 2026 preprint by Zheng et al. uses Gaia XP synthetic photometry and reports that its scaled simulation does not fully reproduce the observed stream morphology; it is not an independent RV test of the knee. (Zheng et al. 2026, preprint, arXiv:2603.02904)

docs.title: 4. Ranked decisive, cheap tests
docs.text:
1. Get independent RVs for a small, clean sample of knee giants. Start with Gaia XP bright giants and cross-match GALAH, Gaia RVS, APOGEE, and any existing southern follow-up spectra. A dozen or more secure giants across both the pre-knee arm and the \(l=-30^\circ\) to \(-45^\circ\) knee would quickly test whether \(v_{\rm los}\) is continuous and whether the knee is one population. The published GALAH candidates at \(l\sim-50^\circ,\ b>30^\circ\) provide a useful anchor, but do not cover the disputed segment.
  2. Make a blind Gaia phase-space plot from the underlying sources. Reproduce the PM–track and distance trends without STREAMFINDER membership weights, then compare the candidate ridge with local field-star controls. Look for bimodality, gaps, scan-law structure, and sensitivity to the membership threshold. This directly tests template joining at low cost.
  3. Forward-model the bar, with the stream and observations treated together. Add a rotating bar over a grid of plausible pattern speeds, bar strengths, orientations, and slowdown histories to the validated cluster model; include the actual release-time distribution. Score sky track, distance, both PM components, RV, and counts jointly. A successful model must reproduce the velocity swing and the modest positional offset; matching only the sky curve is not enough.
  4. Re-run backward tests with a time-dependent barred potential and full cluster covariance. The supplied axisymmetric backtracking result makes this useful. Compare return distances and velocities for knee stars and the \(b<30^\circ\) controls, marginalizing over distance, PM, RV, and bar parameters.
  5. Check close-encounter alternatives only after reconstructing the orbit through the disc. Use the reconstructed stream crossing locations to search for plausible GMC or Sagittarius encounters. These are less compelling without a geometrically close passage, but the impulse estimates show why a specific close encounter should not be dismissed out of hand.

The strongest argument against the bar as the answer: the reported proper-motion difference is so large that, if it represented a persistent velocity offset in one cohort, it should create far more than a 1 kpc displacement over the stated debris age. The bar literature shows that it can restructure streams, but not that a modern \(35\)–\(45\) km s\(^{-1}\) kpc\(^{-1}\) bar produces this particular local combination of PM, track, distance, and RV. The bar is the first mechanism to test; the data do not yet justify calling it the cause.

docs.title: Disagreements, uncertainties and open questions
docs.text:
• The supplied distance, XP, and radial-velocity results favor continuity: the distance declines smoothly rather than stepping, knee giants have an Omega-Cen-compatible metallicity distribution, and \(v_{\rm los}\) is continuous. Those are meaningful checks, but the chemical samples are small and the distal knee lacks published dense spectroscopy.
  • The bar pattern speed is unsettled. Published estimates span roughly 33–40 km s\(^{-1}\) kpc\(^{-1}\) for slow-bar models, while other methods admit faster values. Corotation estimates depend on the adopted rotation curve. The orbit’s being inside or near corotation at some radii does not prove resonant trapping.
  • The bar’s differential effect depends on its orientation at each pericentre, bar growth or slowdown, and the debris’ release phases. A static bar model alone may not capture the history.
  • The halo flattening result from the STREAMFINDER atlas is conditional on that paper’s stream sample and potential family. It does not decide whether an unmodeled triaxial halo can affect this orbit.
  • Survey selection and classification remain unresolved. A continuous CMD-distance and velocity trend is evidence against a simple unrelated foreground group, but does not by itself rule out two kinematically distinct populations selected into one apparent track.
  • The 2026 Omega Cen bar-migration result addresses the cluster’s ancient origin, not the present stream’s last few hundred Myr. It should not be treated as evidence that the observed knee is bar-induced.
