docs.title: Codex review: score-version consistency, provenance and the pooled default (2026-10-17)
docs.text:
Question: the four audit issues and proposed fixes (docs/kb/models/stream_likelihood_versions.md). Codex CLI, effort high, read-only.

One audit premise is incorrect: phase2_variants.py recomputes the requested variants rather than skipping their scores. It still permits mixing: it loads the existing dictionary and replaces only the requested keys. phase2_variants.py:38–65

My priority order is (3), (4), (2), then (1). Adopt S4 for paper inference only after validating and refitting under S4.

  1. (3): enforce provenance before resumption, cache reuse, and comparison. Saving settings alone is insufficient. Paper display resumption keys only on model name and seed; convergence resumption keys only on model label, particle count, and seed. Changing the parameters behind those names can silently retain stale results even without a score-version change. paper_models.py:109–123, particle_convergence.py:35–39,79–89

  2. (4): remove import-time writes immediately. A main() guard fixes the demonstrated overwrite path. Keep reusable model definitions in an inert module and import single_scores directly from its defining module. Currently the knee script imports D1, whose top-level body writes both the D1 JSON and plot. knee_spread_and_frame.py:16, d1_segments.py:21–45

  3. (2): share the estimator, while distinguishing marginals from additive contributions. The present split implementation independently fixes cuts, bin weights, bandwidths, and background widths. That duplication must disappear. obs_split.py:11–29

  4. (1): centralize explicit configurations; avoid making every scientific script follow a changing default. The current wrapper fixes the real catalogue and chord frame. D2 scores simulated observables; the frame checks use alternative coordinates and subsets. Passing those callers through score(m) unchanged would change the experiment. Extract a configurable scoring layer accepting data, frame, and resolved score configuration; keep the current wrapper as its convenience interface. grid4_common.py:15–18,83–94, d2_mock_recovery.py:55–58, rescore_conditional.py:31–38

The correct per-observable definition

Let \(F_A(u,y_A)\) be the foreground joint density marginalized to observable group \(A\), and \(G_A(y_A)\) the corresponding background marginal. Then

\[ p(y_A\mid u)= \frac{(1-\epsilon)F_A(u,y_A)+\epsilon g_u(u)G_A(y_A)} {(1-\epsilon)f_u(u)+\epsilon g_u(u)}. \]

Use identical particles, weights, cuts, and \(f_u\) for every marginal. The conditional background probability is

\[ \beta(u)=\frac{\epsilon g_u(u)} {(1-\epsilon)f_u(u)+\epsilon g_u(u)}, \]

rather than a fresh constant 0.05 for each observable. This follows directly from the implemented joint numerator and denominator. score.py:316–331

These are proper marginal densities under normalized component distributions. Their log scores generally do not sum to the joint log score. Sharing a debris particle and foreground/background membership induces dependence even when each particle’s kernels factorize.

For exact addition, expose a separately named chain decomposition:

\[ \log p(x,\boldsymbol\mu,v\mid u)= \log p(x\mid u)+ \log p(\boldsymbol\mu\mid u,x)+ \log p(v\mid u,x,\boldsymbol\mu). \]

Compute successive ratios of mixture marginals; this automatically updates particle and background probabilities after each conditioning step. The attribution depends on ordering. For missing velocity, omit the velocity factor, matching the existing joint implementation. score.py:321–328

The plotting proposal also needs qualification. return_components currently returns only the evaluated joint density and \(u\) marginal. The plots require arbitrary evaluation grids, individual PM marginals, and intrinsic distributions without per-star errors. The original-coordinate plot additionally reweights particles and smooths in different coordinates; it is an approximate visualization, not simply another evaluation of the joint likelihood. Share particle selection, weights, and marginal evaluators, while retaining that distinction. score.py:330–331, plot_conditional_model.py:35–41, plot_conditional_orig.py:33–51

Minimal robust provenance

Use immutable manifests with content-derived identifiers:

  • Score manifest: schema version; all effective defaults and overrides; weighting; actual bounds and window; bandwidths; cuts; epsilon; hashes of scoring/projection source and relevant dependency versions.
  • Data manifest: hashes of ordered evaluated arrays, errors/covariances, missing-value masks, member identities, selection, units, and frame inputs.
  • Spray manifest: complete resolved physical and numerical parameters, seed, release schedule/count, reference state, potential/profile input hashes, generator code/environment, and output-array hash.

Store manifests beside numerical results under results/plot_data/ or with spray artifacts under results/streams/. Each score record should reference its score/data/spray identifiers. Sidecars for .npy and .npz must include the artifact hash.

The existing settings records only supplied options and a short commit with an optional -dirty suffix. Different dirty trees can therefore have identical provenance; omitted defaults are implicit; changes outside the checked paths are missed. Use actual source-content hashes as identity and retain Git information as descriptive metadata. grid4_common.py:98–123

Use separate keys:

  • Comparison identity: score definition, data, and frame; validate controlled particle resolution and sampling conventions.
  • Job identity: comparison identity plus complete model/spray configuration and seed.

Validate existing records before building done, returning a cached result, or writing anything. Missing provenance means unknown provenance and should fail closed. A new score filename does not validate an old spray cache.

I would omit --force-mix initially. If retained, require per-record identities and explicit partition selection by readers; it must never authorize unlabeled mixed comparisons. Use atomic replacement and a single writer or locking for shared outputs. The paper JSON already uses atomic replacement, but its read/modify/write sequence has no synchronization. paper_models.py:43–48,108–123

Do not treat the historical index as proof. It assigns versions using modification times and inferred commits; its embedded-settings inspection retains version tags without checking complete configuration agreement. Existing escape pilots already store source hashes, but their resume path does not validate those hashes. score_provenance.py:71–90,101–125, compare_escape_recipes.py:77–92

What must be regenerated for an S4 paper

  • Refit the null and barred candidates, then repeat held-out scoring and model selection. Rescoring S2-selected parameters establishes their S4 scores, not their S4 optimality. The paper currently obtains barred parameters from old refinement files and selects the null from saved fit scores. paper_models.py:55–57,101–110
  • Regenerate Figure 2’s likelihood annotations, Figure 3’s cumulative likelihood panel, Figure 5’s sweep rankings, and every likelihood difference in Figure 6, including each matched baseline. These directly consume saved scores or per-star arrays. fig2_models.py:36–46, fig3_residuals.py:55–63, fig5_bar_constraints.py:30–40, fig6_robustness.py:28–61
  • Repeat mock recovery, seed/particle convergence, and uncertainty diagnostics supporting S4 claims. Update both mock generation and scoring: D2 currently generates foreground-only mocks using legacy bin weights. Test full-mixture recovery separately. d2_mock_recovery.py:24–41,55–58
  • Reuse verified sprays when their generating inputs remain appropriate. Data-only Figure 1 needs no score-driven regeneration. Fixed-parameter morphology and residuals may remain; regenerate them when refitting changes their parameters. Figure 4 uses variants at one shared fitted cluster state, so it does not establish independently optimized alternatives. fig1_data.py:40–73, paper_models.py:127–139

Historical experiments can remain documented S2. They cannot substantiate S4-specific calibration or optimality claims. The manuscript’s current method explicitly describes equal-weight chi bins and quotes corresponding recovery and scatter results; those passages require revision if adopting S4. main.tex:164–190

Tests required

For no silent mixing:

  • Resume and append integration tests: independently change weighting, background, an implicit default, data order/value/error/mask, frame, model parameters, seed, resolution, and dirty source contents. Require rejection with output bytes unchanged.
  • Reject missing provenance, stale spray caches, and mixed worker files. Test readers as well as writers.
  • Demonstrate identical jobs resume without recomputation, explicit/default-equivalent settings share identity, and interrupted writes cannot create completed jobs.
  • Test that importing D1 performs no computation or writes.

For marginals matching the joint definition:

  • An independent tiny-particle analytic oracle, with unequal bin populations, correlated PM errors, and mixed velocity availability.
  • Numerical marginalization and normalization tests, including Gaussian foreground mass outside the background box.
  • Background-only, \(\epsilon=1\), \(\epsilon=0\) where defined, empty-selection, and far-from-stream cases.
  • Verify identical \(u\)-conditioned background probability across marginals; verify chain terms sum per star to the joint score.
  • Include a correlated example where the standalone marginal log scores deliberately do not sum to the joint.
  • Check diagnostic modes leave joint scores unchanged and preserve explicitly frozen S2 replay values.

Existing tests cover background fallback, several estimator properties, and version tags. They do not establish these provenance or marginal/chain guarantees; the convergence test compares only two sample sizes. test_score_conditional.py:24–137, test_spray_subset.py:106–122

1. Verified versus assumed. I verified the control flow, likelihood algebra, provenance weaknesses, and figure dependencies cited above. I assume your historical paper artifacts were produced under S2; I did not independently establish their execution history. I could not run tests: the available Python lacks pytest and NumPy. Nothing was modified.

2. Strongest argument against my recommendation. Pooling changes the scientific weighting, not merely numerical convergence: legacy bins give particles weight \(1/(K n_k)\), while pooling weights all selected particles equally. Different branches at the same \(u\) can therefore change relative probability, and contamination remains dependent on \(f_u\). A convergent estimator can converge to an inappropriate spray distribution. Preserving a homogeneous, explicitly finite-resolution S2 analysis could be more defensible than migrating before validating S4. score.py:285–299,323–328

3. What I would check to be sure. Reconstruct artifact-level provenance; reproduce historical S2 scores; measure S4 ranking stability across independent seeds and resolution; run injection/recovery under plausible release histories and contamination; refit with multiple starts; and execute the integration and mathematical tests above. The threshold-based bin selection demonstrates finite-sample instability, but does not by itself prove universal asymptotic non-convergence of every legacy-bin model. score.py:297–299, test_score_conditional.py:113–125

docs.title: Codex review: history matching + stratified search plan (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only.

The oracle does not establish “root = search coverage” uniquely. It adds a high score and adds the truth location to the optimizer starts. Separate those effects with a cheap crossed ablation: original/refitted emulator × original/truth-augmented starts. Missing information is strongly implicated; exclusive causation remains unproved. emulator_benchmark.py:74–85

My ranked recommendation:

  1. Use stratified local search, with reversible global screening. Your score-relative implausibility is an optimisation screen; conventional history matching compares simulator outputs with observations and their uncertainties. (Vernon et al.) Keep excluded regions eligible for exploration and restarts. Making all global exploration conditional on NROY risks preserving the original mistake.

  2. Do not justify \(d\) from z_sd ≈ 1.4. Set physical discrepancy \(d=0\) for this numerical search; calibrate emulator uncertainty separately using signed blocked-validation residuals, their bias, and one-sided upper-tail coverage. The existing statistic divides by combined emulator and simulation uncertainty, so its standard deviation does not directly estimate an emulator-only multiplier. emulator_benchmark.py:47–51 Moreover, T2/T3 truth residuals reach 5.81/6.78σ despite blocked z_sd near 1.4. benchmark.json:770–797, benchmark.json:1322–1349 Treat cutoff 3 as provisional acquisition tuning. Screen against a replicated incumbent’s lower confidence bound minus the declared search tolerance, rather than the largest noisy observation.

  3. Start with 100 total sprays per wave: 60 adaptive local evaluations, 20 whole-domain space-filling evaluations, 10 held-out validations, 10 independent checks—two per angle bin. Use two separated starts per bin and refit after small batches; replenish unsuccessful starts. This allocation is a pilot assumption, not an established optimum. Ten starts leave little budget per start, so share existing observations rather than fitting ten tiny independent GPs. Make shrink/expand decisions noise-aware; the reference TuRBO implementation explicitly warns that noisy observations require different incumbent handling. (TuRBO README)

  4. Fix catalogue routing before spending simulations. The current designer fits stored original scores, the batch worker scores against the real catalogue, and rescoring enumerates fixed batch directories. New mock-directed waves therefore require explicit catalogue-specific score inputs and batch lists throughout. emulator_design.py:58–85, stream_batch.py:89–100, rescore_batch.py:24–47

  5. Use T2 for development; require untouched tests before inference. Freeze rules before the new 20°/33° cases, and vary generating-spray seeds: the existing two catalogues per truth share one generating spray. mock_data.py:99–108 Reusing a common spray library is fair if every competing method receives it and its cost is disclosed. Accept search recovery when a one-sided uncertainty bound on truth score − candidate score is below 100; do not require absolute agreement, since a finite-catalogue optimum can beat truth. Freeze candidates before independent checks.

  6. Separate search completion from interval validation. Provisionally stop after two waves with independently resolved improvement below the tolerance in every competitive bin, plus an exploration/restart audit; reaching the budget means “unresolved” if these fail. Refine angle locations around competing peaks and interval crossings—five bin maxima alone are insufficient. Current profile bands are pointwise GP uncertainty at selected maximizers, not calibrated angle intervals. mock_recovery.py:115–122 Keep total lnL as the acceptance objective; tracks can guide proposals without replacing it.

Separately:

  1. Verified versus assumed: I read the requested files, benchmark records, mock generation, and relevant tests; I did not rerun fits or tests. Existing emulator tests cover a smooth quadratic toy and random-fold coverage, not missed-ridge discovery. test_emulator.py:8–41 The proposed budget, starts and stopping thresholds are assumptions to validate.

  2. Strongest argument against this answer: stratification may spread 100 evaluations too thinly across eight nuisance dimensions. A global acquisition policy could discover the ridge faster. Only matched-budget, independently scored comparisons can establish the benefit.

  3. Needed for confidence: the crossed oracle ablation; matched-budget search comparisons; independent generating-spray repeats; competitive-point resolution checks; direct validation of profile differences; and regression tests for catalogue routing, held-out isolation, duplicate simulation identities, and interrupted/resumed waves.

docs.title: Codex review: selection normalisation of the conditional stream likelihood (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only. Outcome: no change to the score; the selection question is open (user: the model PDF at fixed phase is the likelihood); mock sampler fixed to the current score's mixture.

The code contradicts two premises: the final sample contains stream 54 only, and the mock generator is not an exact sampler of the proposed corrected likelihood. It chooses foreground/background once, then retries only foreground draws. (spray_bar_grid2.py:25–31, mock_data.py:62–79)

My recommendation: implement neither the denominator change nor a closure claim without first specifying the selection being tested. The proposed denominator is mathematically correct for an observed-space box selection, but that does not establish its correctness for this catalogue.

  1. High priority — the diagnosis is conditional on the selection assumption. Both scoring paths use the unrestricted foreground \(u\)-marginal; bounds validate members and normalize the background without restricting foreground particles. Thus they evaluate the stated unselected mixture conditional, rather than its box-selected counterpart. This is a selection mismatch if the data were selected by that box; it is not an intrinsically invalid density over the full foreground support. (score.py:274–290, score.py:329–344, score.py:389–403)

The box is constructed from member extrema; the explicit catalogue cuts instead involve stream identity, latitude and longitude. Containing every member does not make the box the selection function. Treat it as a sensitivity experiment, not an established correction. Padding-dependent normalization can move model preferences, particularly near edges. (grid4_common.py:82–89, spray_bar_grid2.py:25–31)

  1. High priority — use kernel-integrated acceptance, including PM correlation. For an observed-space selection probability \(a(u,w)\), the correct expression is [ L_i^a= \frac{a(u_i,w_i)[(1-\epsilon)f_i(u_i,w_i)+\epsilon g(u_i,w_i)]} {\int a(u_i,w)[(1-\epsilon)f_i(u_i,w)+\epsilon g(u_i,w)]\,dw}. ] For exactly the background box, your proposed denominator follows. For a different footprint, the background integral generally changes too.

Consistency with the implemented numerator requires integrating each Gaussian kernel over the selection. The PM rectangle probability is bivariate, not a product of marginal Gaussian probabilities when covariance is nonzero. Dependence on \(C_i\) is correct when selection acts on measured PMs. An indicator on particle centres describes a different, latent-space selection and cannot replace this integral while leaving the numerator unchanged. (score.py:317–340)

  1. High priority — the mock mismatch survives the proposed fix. Write [ D_i=(1-\epsilon)f_u+\epsilon g_u,\qquad b_i=\epsilon g_u/D_i,\qquad F_i^S=\int_S f_i(u_i,w)\,dw. ] The current sampler generates [ q_{\rm mock}(w\mid u_i) =(1-b_i)\frac{f_i(u_i,w)}{F_i^S}+b_i g_w(w), \quad w\in S, ] because rejection occurs after fixing the component. Your corrected likelihood instead requires background probability [ b_i^S=\frac{\epsilon g_u}{(1-\epsilon)F_i^S+\epsilon g_u}. ] These agree only in special cases. Either use \(b_i^S\), or retry the entire mixture draw, including component selection, after rejection. (mock_data.py:60–80)

  2. Selection details — \(u\) cancels; a velocity cut needs evidence.

A selection depending only on the conditioned \(u_i\) cancels. Do not trim model particles to the observed \(u\) interval merely because observations stop there: kernels centred outside it still contribute inside. However, the implementation uses the observed range to set \(g_u\), so changing that range changes foreground/background mixing. (grid4_common.py:18, score.py:272–273, score.py:332–343)

A velocity-box factor belongs only in measured-velocity members’ denominators if that subset was actually selected by observed velocity. The loader applies an error-quality rule, not a \(0<v<400\) cut; that interval is supplied as background support. Its existence alone does not justify truncating foreground velocities. If catalogue membership depends on velocity even for missing-\(v\) objects, their likelihoods require integrating that selection too. (spray_bar_grid2.py:29–31, grid4_common.py:89–105)

  1. Consequences — rankings and emulator calibration require revalidation. Holding the numerator fixed, the box correction adds [ \Delta\log L=\sum_i\log\frac{(1-\epsilon)f_u(u_i)+\epsilon g_u} {(1-\epsilon)F_i^S+\epsilon g_u}\ge0. ] The increase is model-dependent; aggregate fractions of debris outside the box cannot predict ranking changes. The relevant quantities are kernel- and bin-weighted acceptance probabilities at individual members. (score.py:329–343)

The emulator consumes stored jackknife totals and variances. A changed score requires rescoring every leave-out sample, refitting both emulator mean and noise, and repeating validation. Existing batch code saves full sprays, allowing rescoring without rerunning the dynamics. (emulator_design.py:51–58, emulator_design.py:84–94, stream_batch.py:95–109)

  1. Simpler alternatives — apply known cuts accurately before approximating unknown selection. Transform the explicit sky cuts into acceptance at each \(u\), then integrate the kernels over that region. A verified footprint polygon improves geometric selection, but does not establish PM-dependent membership completeness. Restricting particle centres before smoothing is an approximation whose boundary error must be measured. The actual coordinates are a rotated longitude and polynomial-subtracted latitude, so the Galactic cuts do not generally become a constant across-stream interval. (spray_bar_grid2.py:28, path.py:127–130)

1. Verified versus assumed. I verified the formulas, correlated kernels, component-first rejection, selection cuts and emulator input path by reading the cited code. Existing tests check background-only normalization, cutoff agreement and jackknife agreement; those checks do not establish selected-foreground normalization or sampler closure. (test_score_conditional.py:68–86, test_score_cutoff.py:29–47)

I did not run tests or recompute the quoted debris fractions, bounds or velocity count. The selection derivation assumes acceptance acts on observed quantities and that uncertainties and velocity availability can be conditioned on without an additional selection model.

2. Strongest argument against my recommendation. The current likelihood also lacks a justified STREAMFINDER selection model. If the box closely approximates actual acceptance and acceptance varies substantially between models, leaving the score unchanged could cause more bias than the approximation introduces. That argues for promptly measuring sensitivity, even before the complete selection function is available.

3. Needed for confidence.

  • Numerically integrate the corrected density to one at fixed \(u\), using correlated PM errors, edge particles and mixed velocity availability.
  • Check mock component frequencies against \(b_i^S\), then test repeated-catalogue parameter recovery and coverage under known selection, both with and without correction.
  • Repeat with misspecified selection and varied, independently fixed box boundaries.
  • Recheck exact/cutoff agreement and every jackknife normalization after correction.
  • Rescore existing competitors and inspect acceptance and score changes per member before interpreting emulator profiles.
  • Bound rejection attempts and preserve previous mock outputs: the current loop is unlimited, and catalogue/JSON outputs are overwritten on rerun. (mock_data.py:71–79, mock_data.py:94–99)

docs.title: Codex review: self-consistent solar frame (2026-10-20)
docs.text: Question sent: frames.py + mw_variants.py head + the analysis below. Claude-verified against the papers: GRAVITY 2021 R0 = 8275 +- 9 stat +- 33 sys pc (eq. in sec. 5); Oyama+2024 mu_l = -6.391 +- 0.005 mas/yr; Poder+2023 v_c = 233 +- 7; Zhou+2023 234.04 +- 0.08 +- 1.36; Bennett & Bovy 2019 z_sun = 20.8 +- 0.3 pc. Feng+2026 not checked.

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Context: we fit the omega Cen tidal stream ("stream 54", phi1 -5..30 deg, d ~5.4 kpc) with test-particle sprays in a rotating-bar Milky Way (Hunter et al.-type potential: bar + discs + halo; free parameters bar angle, pattern speed, bar amplitude/size, omega Cen distance, v_c(R0) via halo normalisation, halo flattening q). Observables: sky track, Gaia PMs, v_los. The solar frame converts observables <-> Galactocentric. Current frame (code below): R0 = 8.178 kpc, z_sun = 0, Vsun = (11.1, 252.24, 7.25) km/s held FIXED while v_c(R0) of the potential is a free parameter (220-240 in fits; best fits pile at the lower edge 220-223). 252.24 = 240 + 12.24 (Schoenrich+2010 V). Problem: (1) Vsun is not tied to v_c, so v_c + V_pec is inconsistent whenever vc != 240; (2) Vsun/R0 implies mu_SgrA = 252.24/(4.740478.178) = 6.507 mas/yr vs measured 6.411 +- 0.008 (Reid & Brunthaler 2020, 2020ApJ...892...39R).

My proposal: constrain V_tot = vc + V_pec by the Sgr A* proper motion: V_tot = 4.74047 * 6.411 * R0. With R0 = 8.178 (GRAVITY 2019, 2019A&A...625L..10G) -> 248.5 km/s; with R0 ~8.275 (GRAVITY 2021, 2021A&A...647A..59G; value from memory, please verify) -> 251.5. Then let v_c vary in a literature band (Eilers+2019 2019ApJ...871..120E: 229.0 +- 0.2 stat, 2-5% sys, at R0 = 8.122) and V_pec = V_tot - v_c. U_sun = 11.1, W_sun = 7.25 (Schoenrich+2010). Candidate band v_c 229-237.

Questions (be critical; verify numbers against the papers, give arXiv/DOI): 1. What is the current best R0 (GRAVITY 2021/2022, Do+2019 Keck) with errors? Which should we adopt and why? 2. Is fixing V_tot from mu_SgrA and floating v_c (with V_pec = V_tot - v_c) the right self-consistent parametrisation? Or should we instead fix V_pec (Schoenrich 12.24, or other values, e.g. Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016) and let V_tot = v_c + V_pec float, putting a prior from mu_SgrA? Which is more defensible for a stream fit? Note: in a barred, non-axisymmetric potential the LSR / v_c(R0) is ill-defined; V_pec relative to "v_c" depends on the bar. What do people do (e.g. Ibata+2019 omega Cen/Fimbulthul, Bonaca/Koposov stream fits, Vasiliev+2021 Sgr, Pal 5 bar fits Pearson+2017, Bonaca+2020)? 3. Eilers+2019 v_c is at R0 = 8.122 and has slope -1.7 km/s/kpc; how to transfer to R0 = 8.178 or 8.275? Is Eilers the right reference, vs Zhou+2023 / Ou+2024 / Gaia DR3-based curves? Give a defensible v_c(R0) band. 4. z_sun: we use 0; is ~20.8 pc (Bennett & Bovy 2019) worth including for a stream at 5 kpc? Impact estimate. 5. The potential (bar + discs) was built for R0 = 8.178 (v_c is set at that radius). If R0 changes, what else must change consistently (bar angle definition relative to Sun-GC line, v_c normalisation radius)? 6. Recommend one concrete self-consistent frame (R0, z_sun, U,V,W or V_tot, v_c band) with justification, and list failure modes.

Code (src/ocen_dm/streams/frames.py):

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Research mode used: ordinary Codex web research fallback Native Deep Research: unavailable from this invocation path Scientific source rules: yes Model effort: high Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
• Use the Sun’s total Galactocentric velocity as a frame parameter, independently of the potential’s circular speed. Holding \(V_{\rm tot}\) fixed while varying \(v_c\) is consistent; it changes the implied \(V_{\rm pec}\). The problem is interpreting \(252.24\) as \(v_c+12.24\) throughout the fit.
  • Adopt \(R_0\simeq8.277\) kpc as the fiducial distance. GRAVITY’s 2021 optical-aberration correction superseded its 2019 value of 8.178 kpc. Its published 2024 multi-star fit remains at \(8.2759\pm0.0086\) kpc formally; retain the approximately 0.033 kpc systematic floor. Keck’s lower distance remains a substantive disagreement. GRAVITY 2021, GRAVITY 2024, Table B.1.
  • Your Sgr A* calculation is correct: Reid & Brunthaler’s measurement gives \(V_{\rm tot}=248.539\) km/s at 8.178 kpc and \(251.548\) km/s at 8.277 kpc. However, a 2024 VERA/VLBA analysis gives a slightly different proper motion, corresponding to \(250.763\) km/s at 8.277 kpc. Use an astrometric prior or sensitivity analysis rather than treating either central value as exact. Reid & Brunthaler 2020, Oyama et al. 2024.
  • A hard \(229\!-\!237\) km/s interval is narrower than the defensible external uncertainty. I recommend a working prior \(v_{c,0}(R_0)\sim\mathcal N(235,7^2)\) km/s, with approximately \(220\!-\!250\) km/s available for exploration. This is a synthesis for this application, not a published combined measurement.
  • Include \(z_\odot=20.8\) pc. Its effect is small but relevant to precise stream modelling. Changing both \(R_0\) and \(V_{\rm tot}\) to the recommended values changes your present \(V_y\) by only \(-0.69\) km/s, so the preference for \(220\!-\!223\) km/s cannot be attributed to the solar velocity without controlled refits.

docs.title: 1. Distance to the Galactic centre
docs.text:
The relevant measurements are:

Analysis \(R_0\), kpc Uncertainty and assumptions GRAVITY 2019 \(8.178\pm0.013_{\rm stat}\pm0.022_{\rm sys}\) S2 orbit; formal statistical errors approximately \(1\sigma\). This predates the optical-aberration correction. Paper. GRAVITY 2021 \(8.275\pm0.009_{\rm stat}\pm0.033_{\rm sys}\) Corrected GRAVITY astrometry; systematic contributions combined in quadrature. Your remembered value is correct. Equation 38. GRAVITY 2022 \(8.277\pm0.009_{\rm stat}\) Joint S2/S29/S38/S55 fit; paper quotes systematics of approximately 0.030 kpc, referring to the 2021 analysis. Paper. GRAVITY 2024 \(8.2759\pm0.0086_{\rm formal}\) Published four-star fit, with Schwarzschild-precession parameter fitted. This is not a new 8.6-pc total-accuracy claim. Table B.1. Do et al. 2019, GR fixed \(7.946\pm0.050_{\rm stat}\pm0.032_{\rm sys}\) Marginalized 68% interval; systematic term from reference-frame jackknife. Paper and supplement. Do et al. 2019, redshift parameter free \(7.959\pm0.059_{\rm stat}\pm0.032_{\rm sys}\) Table 1 posterior estimate. The main text also quotes the maximum-likelihood distance, 7.971 kpc, with these errors. These explain several apparently conflicting quotations of this paper. Table 1.

Recommendation: use 8.277 kpc, with a working distance prior of approximately [ R_0\sim\mathcal N(8.277,\;0.034^2)\ {\rm kpc}, ] conditional on accepting the GRAVITY calibration and identifying Sgr A* with the model centre. The 0.034 kpc width approximates the quadrature combination of the 2021 statistical and systematic terms; it is not an uncertainty obtained by averaging successive GRAVITY papers.

The reason to prefer this scale is the corrected interferometric astrometry and its stability in subsequent multi-star fits. The 2021 paper attributes the earlier GRAVITY shift to optical aberrations and investigates the Keck discrepancy: radial velocities and astrometric reference-frame differences can explain substantial portions, but the authors do not establish a complete, independently demonstrated resolution. GRAVITY 2021, §5 and Appendix C.

The Keck–GRAVITY difference is approximately 4–5 nominal standard deviations, depending on which Do fit is compared and treating systematic terms as Gaussian. Thus, the above narrow prior does not cover all credible cross-instrument uncertainty. An external check from bar-star kinematics gives \(8.23\pm0.12\) kpc, with bootstrap uncertainty and a deliberately broad solar-angular-speed uncertainty; it supports the general 8.2–8.3 kpc scale without resolving the instrumental disagreement. Leung et al., 2023 journal volume; online December 2022.

I found no later verified distance result that materially supersedes this GRAVITY scale as of 2026-10-20.

docs.title: 2. Parametrisation: separate the observer from the gravitational field
docs.text:
Define the circular-speed parameter explicitly through the azimuthally averaged potential: [ \Phi_0(R,z)\equiv\langle\Phi(R,\phi,z,t)\rangle_\phi,\qquad v_{c,0}^2(R)=R\,\partial_R\Phi_0(R,0). ]

This quantity is well defined in a barred model. What is generally unavailable is a circular orbit, and hence a unique circular-orbit LSR, in the full non-axisymmetric potential.

The frame transformation requires the actual solar velocity: [ \boldsymbol v_\odot=(U_\odot,V_{\rm tot},W_\odot). ] It does not require a choice of \(v_{c,0}\). Consequently:

Fixing—or tightly constraining—\(V_{\rm tot}\), while independently varying \(v_{c,0}\), is a consistent parametrisation.

You can define [ V_{\rm pec,0}\equiv V_{\rm tot}-v_{c,0}(R_0) ] as a derived quantity. Its interpretation is motion relative to your axisymmetric reference potential.

For a local stellar LSR, a more informative decomposition is [ V_{\rm tot}=v_{c,0}+v_{\rm stream}+V_{\rm pec,local}. ] Here \(v_{\rm stream}\) represents the local departure from axisymmetric circular rotation. Setting \(v_{\rm stream}=0\) and fixing \(V_{\rm pec,local}\) is an additional physical assumption.

Schönrich, Binney & Dehnen report [ (U,V,W)\odot= (11.1^{+0.69},\,12.24\pm0.47,\, 7.25^{+0.37}_{-0.36})\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}, ] with additional estimated systematics approximately \((1,2,0.5)\) km/s. These are model-based local-kinematic estimates, not a requirement that every Galactic potential satisfy \(V_{\rm tot}-v_{c,0}=12.24\). Schönrich et al. 2010.

Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard’s review adopts approximately \((10,11,7)\) km/s for the local peculiar motion, with quoted uncertainties \((1,2,0.5)\) km/s, while discussing potentially appreciable streaming relative to circular rotation. Their adopted \(V\) is 11, not 24 km/s. Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, §5.3.3.

For this stream fit, I favour \((R_0,V_{\rm tot},v_{c,0})\) with external frame priors. Fixing \(V_{\rm pec}=12.24\) and imposing Sgr A* is mathematically valid, but it imports a stronger local-disc assumption. At \(R_0=8.277\) kpc, those two constraints force [ v_{c,0}\simeq251.548-12.24=239.31\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}. ] A fit advertised as freely measuring \(v_c\) would then be strongly constrained externally.

docs.title: The Sgr A* constraint
docs.text:
Using the magnitude of the longitudinal component, not the total two-dimensional proper motion, [ \Omega_\odot\equiv V_{\rm tot}/R_0 \simeq4.74047\,|\mu_{l}| =30.3912\pm0.0379\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}\,kpc^{-1}}. ] The measured motion is negative; the solar rotation speed is positive. The conversion assumes negligible intrinsic longitudinal motion of Sgr A and the usual nearly aligned geometry. The radio uncertainty is \(1\sigma\). Reid & Brunthaler 2020.

My calculated values are:

\(R_0\), kpc \(V_{\rm tot}\), km/s 8.178 248.539 8.275 251.487 8.277 251.548

At fixed 8.277 kpc, the formal radio contribution is only 0.314 km/s. Including a 0.034 kpc distance uncertainty gives approximately 1.08 km/s, assuming independent, approximately Gaussian errors.

A relevant update is Oyama et al.’s combined VERA/VLBA result, [ \mu_{l}=-6.391\pm0.005\ {\rm mas\,yr^{-1}}, ] with formal \(1\sigma\) uncertainty. It gives 250.763 km/s at 8.277 kpc, 0.785 km/s below* the Reid–Brunthaler value. It reuses earlier VLBA data, so the two measurements should not be combined as independent constraints. Oyama et al. 2024, §5.2.

I would retain Reid–Brunthaler for a clearly documented fiducial frame, propagate its uncertainty, and repeat the inference with Oyama’s value. Alternatively, an explicitly conservative additional 1 km/s frame-systematic nuisance term covers this difference; that is my proposed modelling allowance, not a published measurement.

docs.title: What stream papers actually do
docs.text:
There is no single convention across the examples.

Study Verified treatment Implication Ibata et al. 2019, Fimbulthul \(R_0=8.122\) kpc, \(z_\odot=17\) pc, circular speed 220 km/s, plus Schönrich peculiar motion. Methods. Your quoted solar parameters reproduce their stated choice. This is a historical adopted frame, not a modern Sgr A* calibration. Koposov, Rix & Hogg 2010, GD-1 Link the LSR speed to the fitted potential; add fixed Dehnen–Binney peculiar motion, including \(V_{\rm pec}=5.25\) km/s. §5. An example of the alternative parametrisation, under older assumptions. Pearson et al. 2017, barred Pal 5 Fixed solar position \(R_0=8.0\) kpc and total tangential velocity 244 km/s; model circular speed approximately 220 km/s. §1.3. Fixed total observer velocity in a bar experiment. Bonaca et al. 2020, Pal 5 \(R_0=8.1\) kpc; circular speed 220 plus azimuthal offset 24, giving total 244 km/s. §4.1. Again, the offset is not Schönrich’s 12.24. Vasiliev, Belokurov & Erkal 2021, Sgr Fixed solar position \((-8.1,0,0.02)\) kpc and velocity \((12.9,245.6,7.8)\) km/s; halo normalization chosen to give circular speed near 235 km/s. §§2, 3.3. Separates total solar velocity from potential normalization.

These precedents establish that your proposed separation is normal practice; their numerical choices should not be treated as independent measurements of today’s preferred frame.

docs.title: 3. Circular-speed evidence and transferring Eilers
docs.text:
For a fixed published physical curve, Eilers’ linear fit gives [ v_c(R)=229.0-1.7(R-8.122)\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}, ] hence 228.905 km/s at 8.178 kpc and 228.740 km/s at 8.275 kpc. The fitted normalization and slope have formal errors 0.2 km/s and 0.1 km/s/kpc; the paper estimates 2–5% systematic effects on speed. Those percentages are not a calibrated confidence interval. Eilers et al. 2019.

But changing the assumed solar frame in their inference is a different operation. Eilers used \(R_0=8.122\) kpc and \(V_{\rm tot}\simeq245.8\) km/s, inferred from Sgr A*, without requiring a peculiar-motion decomposition. Moving to \(V_{\rm tot}=251.55\) changes inferred stellar azimuthal velocities and Jeans terms. It cannot be represented by the \(-0.26\) km/s radial correction alone. Eilers et al., §3.

The later evidence is:

Source Relevant result Qualification Zhou et al. 2023 \(234.04\pm0.08_{\rm stat}\pm1.36_{\rm sys}\) km/s at \(R_0=8.122\) kpc Formal fit error and assessed systematic shifts; axisymmetric Jeans analysis, \(V_{\rm tot}=245.6\). The scalar error’s coverage is not separately specified in the result passage. Paper. Ou et al. 2024 At \(R=8.19\) kpc, \(232.83^{+0.56}_{-0.55}\) km/s Table 1 bootstrap statistical errors; additional systematic effects are several percent. Uses \(R_0=8.178\), \(V_y=247.3\). Paper. Põder et al. 2023, Gaia DR3 \(233\pm7\) km/s, using the 8.277-kpc scale Bayesian propagation of distance and tracer-profile nuisance parameters; curve errors use the 16th–84th posterior percentiles. Paper. Feng et al. 2026 \(236.8\pm0.8\) km/s at \(R_0=8.275\) kpc From an averaged curve combining their Cepheids with previous work after frame adjustments. The quoted scalar error has no explicit coverage statement; it is not a comprehensive systematic bound. Published 7 January 2026. Publisher.

Eilers remains a useful reference, but not a sufficient narrow prior. The later studies are not independent enough to justify a simple inverse-variance average. They share Gaia information, sometimes tracer samples, and assumptions about equilibrium, axisymmetry, density gradients and distances.

For this application, my recommendation is:

\[ \boxed{v_{c,0}(R_0)\sim\mathcal N(235,7^2)\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}.} \]

The width is a working prior standard deviation, deliberately broader than formal fit errors. Approximately \(220\!-\!250\) km/s is a useful exploration interval, not a hard literature confidence interval. Your \(229\!-\!237\) interval is reasonable for a focused sensitivity grid, but too restrictive as the sole allowed range.

This caution is supported by Koop et al.: their Gaia DR3 analysis finds an approximately 8 km/s difference between curves inferred above and below the plane, and tests show that equilibrium, axisymmetric Jeans reconstruction becomes less robust at large radii. This does not invalidate the solar-radius measurements; it limits how literally to interpret tiny formal errors. Koop et al. 2024.

docs.title: 4. Solar height
docs.text:
Bennett & Bovy obtain \(z_\odot=20.8\pm0.3\) pc after accounting for asymmetry in the local vertical density distribution. The quoted uncertainty comes from their MCMC analysis; the result passage does not explicitly define its coverage. It is a local-midplane measurement, not a universal 0.3-pc uncertainty in the plane of the entire Galaxy. Bennett & Bovy 2019.

Include it, while retaining the distinction between a local measured midplane and the symmetry plane of your idealized discs.

My geometric estimates are:

  • The displacement scale at 5.4 kpc is \(20.8/5400=0.00385\) rad, or 0.221°.
  • Astropy also tilts the axes by approximately \(z_\odot/R_0=\mathbf{0.144^\circ}\).
  • Near ω Cen, using approximately \(l=309.1^\circ,b=15^\circ,d=5.4\) kpc, that transformation changes Galactocentric \(z\) by about 12.5 pc, and \(x\) by about 3.5 pc, relative to \(z_\odot=0\).
  • Rotating a 200 km/s velocity through 0.0025 rad produces a component change of order 0.5 km/s.

The 0.221° figure is a scale estimate, not a predicted stream-track displacement. Transforming identical observables into a frame and back leaves them unchanged. The scientific effect comes from changing their position and velocity relative to the model’s disc plane and then evolving them. Astropy documents the height-dependent tilt explicitly. Astropy frame definition.

docs.title: 5. What changes when \(R_0\) changes?
docs.text:
A new observer distance does not require rescaling every component of a potential expressed in physical units. Distinguish changing the observer from rebuilding a Galactic mass model.

For your supplied formulation:

  1. Recompute the progenitor’s Galactocentric phase space from the same observables. Use the same frame for projecting every stream realization.

  2. Specify the normalization radius. If the fitted parameter means \(v_{c,0}\) at the new solar radius, impose [ c=\frac{v_{c,\rm target}^2-v_{c,\rm baryon}^2(R_{\rm new})} {v_{c,\rm halo,unit}^2(R_{\rm new})}. ] Alternatively, retaining normalization at 8.178 kpc is valid, but then the parameter is \(v_{c,0}(8.178)\), and literature comparisons require evaluating the model at the actual solar radius.

  3. Retain the definition of bar angle relative to the present Sun–GC line. Moving the Sun radially does not itself change that angle. A reflection of the \(x\)-axis changes azimuth and rotation-sign conventions, so literature angles and pattern-speed signs require explicit translation.

  4. Disc lengths, bar size and masses need not automatically change. If their adopted values were inferred from angular observables under the old distance, recalibrating those observational constraints is a separate modelling exercise. Likewise, a physical pattern speed does not automatically rescale because the observer moved.

  5. Keep the axisymmetric reference identifiable when varying the bar. If the added perturbation has exactly zero azimuthal mean, its amplitude leaves \(v_{c,0}\) unchanged. If size/amplitude changes alter the mean mass distribution, include that change in the normalization.

Hunter et al. themselves define circular speed through the axisymmetric potential and distinguish it from the Sun’s total speed, discussing peculiar motion and streaming as contributions to the difference. Their synthetic-observer convention is not a solar-frame recommendation for your data. Hunter et al. 2024, §§3.3–4.1.

A small precision point: Astropy’s galcen_distance is the Sun–centre distance; the cylindrical solar radius is \(\sqrt{D_{\rm GC}^2-z_\odot^2}\). Their difference here is only 0.026 pc, negligible for the potential normalization. Astropy API.

docs.title: 6. Concrete recommendation
docs.text:
For a fiducial realization, I recommend:

Quantity Adopt \(R_0\) 8.277 kpc \(z_\odot\) 20.8 pc Solar Cartesian \(v_x\) in the supplied Astropy convention +11.1 km/s Solar total \(v_y\) 251.548 km/s Solar Cartesian \(v_z\) +7.25 km/s Potential parameter \(v_{c,0}\) of the azimuthally averaged potential at the solar radius Working circular-speed prior \(\mathcal N(235,7^2)\) km/s Derived azimuthal offset \(V_{\rm pec,0}=251.548-v_{c,0}\)

At \(v_{c,0}=235\), the derived offset is 16.55 km/s. Across \(229\!-\!237\), it is 22.55–14.55 km/s. Those values should be labelled relative to the axisymmetric reference, without claiming they directly measure the local stellar peculiar motion.

For inference, propagate \(R_0\) and the Sgr A* angular-speed uncertainty jointly, preserving [ V_{\rm tot}=\Omega_\odot R_0. ] Retain conventional \(U,W\) centrally, but allow uncertainties of order 1–2 km/s in sensitivity analyses rather than treating them as exact.

One qualification about \(W\): this recommendation imposes the longitudinal Sgr A constraint. It does not exactly impose its latitude motion. Reid–Brunthaler measure \(\mu_b=-0.219\pm0.007\) mas/yr; if Sgr A is fixed vertically, that corresponds to a projected solar vertical speed near 8.6 km/s at 8.277 kpc, with approximately 0.3 km/s uncertainty after including distance. Strict use of both radio components requires projecting the complete velocity vector through the adopted geometry and constraining \(W\) accordingly. Keeping 7.25 is a conventional choice whose approximately 1 km/s discrepancy should be included in the frame sensitivity analysis. Reid & Brunthaler 2020.

docs.title: Disagreements, uncertainties and failure modes
docs.text:
• The old frame is observationally questionable, not algebraically impossible. At \(v_c=220\), its \(V_{\rm tot}=252.24\) implies an offset of 32.24 km/s. Whether that is plausible depends on the reference LSR and streaming assumptions.
  • The lower-edge preference may survive the correction. At fixed \(R_0=8.178\), correcting \(V_y\) changes it by \(-3.70\) km/s—up to 0.145 mas/yr at 5.4 kpc. Adopting both the new distance and new velocity changes \(V_y\) by only \(-0.69\) km/s—up to 0.027 mas/yr. These are fixed-phase-space projection sensitivities, not predictions for refitted streams.
  • Frame changes can be absorbed by distance and dynamics. Solar reflex proper motion scales as \(V_\perp/d\); ω Cen distance, halo normalization, flattening and bar parameters can compensate each other. A boundary optimum is not a secure circular-speed measurement.
  • Do not double-count external information. Rotation curves already depend on adopted solar frames. A tiny-error circular-speed prior plus Sgr A* and a fixed peculiar-motion prior can impose incompatible assumptions or reuse information.
  • The local force does not determine the inner orbit. Changing only halo normalization may drive \(v_c\) downward to compensate for the adopted baryonic mass, bar structure or radial force profile. Positive halo normalization also imposes a baryonic floor.
  • Keep density flattening distinct from potential flattening. Your \(q\) is a halo-density axis ratio; constraints quoted for \(q_\Phi\) cannot be applied directly.
  • The distance and radio systematics remain unresolved at their formal precision. GRAVITY versus Keck is the larger issue; the two recent radio reductions differ by about 0.8 km/s in inferred \(V_{\rm tot}\).
  • A single short stream segment may not separate all these freedoms. Stripping history and time-dependent bar dynamics can affect the inference. The decisive scientific check is a set of controlled refits separating the \(R_0\), \(V_{\rm tot}\) and \(z_\odot\) changes, followed by fits with frame uncertainties marginalized.

docs.title: Codex speed review 2026 10 11
docs.text: The current optimization violates the hard requirement as written. make_spray now returns only particles younger than 700 Myr, so callers that inspect the full trailing stream receive fewer particles than before; the cutoff happens in spray_unwrapped before its result is returned to make_spray grid4_common.py:53–55 spray.py:121–129. For the likelihood alone, this pruning is equivalent when age_max=700: the scorer selects chi > 0 and age < age_max score.py:250–253. But that does not preserve the complete returned stream. Treat the age cutoff as C under the PI’s strict requirement; it is A only if the requirement is explicitly limited to score-relevant particles.

docs.title: Ranked speedups
docs.text:
1. Keep the pruning only if the PI accepts score-equivalent output. Initial conditions are generated before the mask is applied, including spin velocities, and the release epochs and progenitor orbit are computed before pruning spray.py:111–120 spray.py:121–129. The regression test checks exact equality for the retained particles against two stored runs, and checks a separate full-versus-subset run test_spray_subset.py:17–46. A for the retained subset, subject to the coverage limits below; C for preserving the full returned stream.

The scoring guard is not reliable: it hardcodes 700 and infers truncation from the largest returned age grid4_common.py:58–62. A spray cut at 500 Myr can therefore be scored with age_max=600 without an error; a shorter release window can also make an untruncated spray appear “cut.” Store the cutoff explicitly with the model and validate age_max against that metadata, or require the caller to pass the cutoff. Add tests for cutoffs below and above 700 and for short windows.

  1. Reuse deterministic setup across seeds. Within one model, host_potential, the backward and forward centre orbits, release-time interpolation, and rj_vj_R are recomputed before particles are drawn and integrated grid4_common.py:49–54 spray.py:111–120 spray.py:22–39. Cache or pass these arrays and the host potential across seeds for the same parameters. A, if the cache key includes all inputs that affect them and cached arrays are reused unchanged. Do not reuse across changed host, distance, frame, release settings, or mass profile.

  2. Reduce trajectory samples only as a measured approximation. Each particle currently has 240 trajectory samples; chi is integrated with a trapezoid over those samples, while psi is computed in the same per-particle loop spray.py:96–108 spray.py:136–143. Fewer samples change the numerical quadrature for chi, so classify this B, not A. Benchmark ntraj values such as 120, 60, and 30 against 240. A reasonable proposed acceptance test is, across fixed representative models and seeds, maximum per-star log-likelihood change below 0.1 and total log-likelihood change below 1; also report maximum changes in stream observables relative to the measurement errors. The code does not establish how much runtime is trajectory output versus force integration, so measure both elapsed time and memory before expecting a large gain.

Skipping psi is a small A opportunity for the make_spray path: it returns neither psi nor any quantity derived from it grid4_common.py:53–55 spray.py:142–144. Make it an opt-in calculation in spray_unwrapped so its existing default return remains intact.

  1. Parallelize independent models for throughput. Processes can run separate model evaluations with fewer AGAMA threads each; this does not make one evaluation faster and does not change its mathematical inputs. A for output, expected benefit only for throughput. Benchmark process/thread combinations on the target Mac and guard against oversubscribing AGAMA/BLAS threads.

  2. Keep the current integration tolerance unless the PI accepts a numerical bound. The packet reports that changing accuracy from 1e-8 to 1e-6 changed total log likelihood by 1.7, and 1e-5 changed it by −20 packet:2017–2024. These are B changes, not bit-identical output. The measurements do not establish that either tolerance stays within a stated bound across models and seeds.

I would not replace the rotating host with an axisymmetric approximation: host_potential explicitly builds a rotating bar restricted.py:60–89, so dropping it changes the model (C). The source shows a moving, fixed satellite potential is included in the particle orbit spray.py:127–129; it does not show that this force evaluation is a dominant cost. Profile before simplifying either potential.

AGAMA units: agama_kpc() calls setUnits(mass=1, length=1, velocity=1) every time restricted.py:30–34. The spray path calls it again after constructing the host, including from spray_unwrapped and rj_vj_R restricted.py:59 spray.py:24 spray.py:109–119. Those calls request identical units, so the warning alone does not prove a scaling error. But another module sets AGAMA length to 0.001 for pc units backends.py:177. Avoid mixing those paths in one process; verify units with a test that compares potential forces before and after repeated initialization and after importing/running the pc-unit backend.

docs.title: Verified by reading the code
docs.text:
• The current call path masks particles after drawing their initial conditions, and make_spray returns only the trailing arm spray.py:119–129 grid4_common.py:53–55.
  • The scorer filters by chi > 0 and age < age_max score.py:250–253.
  • The regression tests cover two stored configurations, one using the Ibata frame, and a separate subset comparison without spin; stored-run checks skip when their files are absent test_spray_subset.py:17–46 test_spray_subset.py:24–34.

docs.title: Assumptions and strongest argument against my recommendation
docs.text: I assume independent particle integrations produce the same results regardless of which other particles are in the AGAMA orbit call. The test’s bitwise comparison supports that for its cases, but it does not cover spin or peri-centred release. The strongest argument against making cutoff pruning the top speedup is that it breaks the stated full-stream contract and narrows what downstream callers can inspect, even though it preserves the likelihood’s selected subset.

docs.title: What I would check to be sure
docs.text:
• Add exact subset tests for spin, peri-centred release, both frames, and cutoff-boundary ages; ensure the stored-reference tests run rather than skip.
  • Profile time inside AGAMA particle integration versus trajectory sampling, potential evaluation, and Python post-processing.
  • Validate any reduced ntraj and relaxed accuracy against the proposed likelihood and observable thresholds over representative parameter points and seeds.
  • Test AGAMA unit initialization with potentials already constructed and with the pc-unit backend in the same process.

docs.title: Codex review: speeding up the AGAMA spray (2026-10-19)
docs.text:
Codex CLI, effort high, read-only; full source of spray.py, restricted.py, mw_variants.py and make_spray supplied.

The rotating-frame premise is partly wrong: the local AGAMA implementation of Cartesian Omega=... still integrates in inertial coordinates and rotates the potential during force evaluation. Do not expect a major gain from changing frames alone. Combining potential components is a separate optimization. AGAMA orbit.cpp:183, upstream implementation.

My recommendation: validate accuracy=1e-6 first, benchmark dprkn8 second, then investigate combining the host components. Defer satellite truncation and particle reduction.

  1. Particle accuracy 1e-6: highest-confidence speed opportunity, approximately 1.9×. That is 108/57 from the supplied measurements, not an independently reproduced benchmark. The parameter reaches particle integration while progenitor integration remains at 1e-12, which makes this a relatively isolated experiment. [packet:2018], spray.py:121, spray.py:156.

Risk/test: numerical errors can systematically favour particular models despite remaining below seed scatter in one example. Compare identical seeds and release epochs at both tolerances across central, boundary, strong-bar and flattened-halo models. Measure paired score changes, changes in model-to-model score differences, and observable distributions. This requires statistical equivalence, not bit identity.

  1. Benchmark method="dprkn8": plausible additional 1.2–1.3×, unmeasured here. AGAMA documents that approximate improvement; the spray currently leaves method unspecified. Its lower-order dense output makes trajectory-derived quantities and final interpolated velocities explicit validation targets. AGAMA reference.tex:1154, AGAMA reference.tex:2180, spray.py:156.

Risk/test: benchmark it separately at both tolerances against a tighter dop853 reference, retaining the existing trajectory sampling. Check chi, final observables and scores. Do not assume its gain multiplies independently with the tolerance gain.

  1. Combine host components before attempting a frame rewrite: potentially substantial, but no defensible speed multiplier yet. The production path evaluates an axisymmetric component plus separately scaled positive and negative baryonic components. For constant bar speed and size, a static combined representation wrapped in one rotation can be tested while retaining inertial particle integration and the existing satellite trajectory. Slowing bars and additional LMC/spiral terms need separate treatment. restricted.py:83, restricted.py:96, restricted.py:106, restricted.py:40.

Risk/test: re-expansion introduces force and Hessian errors; Hessians also determine release radii. Compare potential, force and Hessian over the occupied spatial/time domain, including pericentres, the plane and expansion boundaries; then run matched sprays. Preserve the original release calculation initially to isolate integration error. spray.py:32, spray.py:128.

If using Omega, rotate both positions and inertial velocity components consistently; do not subtract Ω × r from AGAMA’s velocity convention. Satellite-centre interpolation needs separate care because a centre-position derivative in rotating coordinates differs from those velocity components. AGAMA orbit.cpp:104, AGAMA reference.tex:510.

  1. Thread/process tuning: expect limited throughput improvement if eight workers already occupy the available compute capacity. AGAMA parallelizes across orbits; this redistributes the same work rather than reducing force evaluations. AGAMA interface_python.cpp:7871.

Risk/test: compare eight identical sprays using worker/thread combinations (8,1), (4,2), (2,4), (1,8). Measure completed sprays/hour, peak memory and output identity. Single-spray latency is insufficient. Hardware saturation and scaling remain assumptions.

  1. Cheaper satellite treatment: investigate only after a matched ablation measures its cost. Timing inside agama.orbit does not distinguish host force, satellite force, centre interpolation and integration overhead: the particle call receives their combined potential. spray.py:144, spray.py:156.

If satellite evaluation occupies fraction f of runtime, eliminating that cost has an optimistic ceiling of 1/(1−f). Risk/test: a distance threshold alone does not establish negligible cumulative deflection or prevent later encounters. Compare several switch radii, retain/re-enable gravity for returning particles, and check scores, stream length, widths and tails. The current calculation retains satellite gravity throughout. spray.py:144.

  1. Fewer particles: approximately proportional runtime savings, with a direct statistical cost. Under ordinary Monte Carlo scaling, halving particles increases scatter by roughly √2; bias correction does not remove that variance. The existing jackknife is a bias correction, not a replacement for seed replication. score_bias.py:75.

Risk/test: establish both bias and variance using independent replicates at 128k, 256k and a larger reference. Preserve the score definition: the wrapper defaults to pooled scoring, while training records also use fixed and legacy chi bins. grid4_common.py:95, training_set.py:189. Use fewer particles for screening only until those comparisons justify final inference.

Other proposed changes have little demonstrated upside:

  • Lower trajsize is not result-equivalent. chi is a trapezoidal integral over trajectory samples and controls particle selection/binning. Two samples can preserve endpoints while changing the score. spray.py:160, score.py:299.
  • Python vectorization, release-radius tuning and construction-only caching: approximately 1% maximum benefit in the supplied 108-second benchmark, assuming its timing attribution is complete. Those operations sit outside the measured 107 seconds in orbit integration. [packet:2018].
  • dtype/der: the local AGAMA default already stores trajectories as float32; der=True requests additional deviation-vector calculations. The spray supplies neither option. Casting saved arrays to float64 does not recover discarded precision. AGAMA interface_python.cpp:7524, spray.py:156, training_set.py:186.

1. Verified versus assumed

Verified by reading: parameter propagation, combined host/satellite integration, trajectory-dependent chi, AGAMA’s local frame/storage conventions, and existing regression assertions. Subset and chunk tests demand exact array equality; stored-reference tests can skip when their files are absent. tests/test_spray_subset.py:35, tests/test_spray_subset.py:66, tests/test_spray_subset.py:86.

Assumed: the supplied timings and 30–45 score scatter are representative; production uses the inspected AGAMA implementation; eight workers substantially occupy the machine. I did not reproduce benchmarks or run the regression suite.

2. Strongest argument against my answer

Relaxed tolerance could introduce parameter-dependent bias that survives seed averaging and shifts inferred parameters. A more expensive implementation effort that preserves forces could therefore be preferable even with a smaller speed gain. The release calculation’s dependence on host Hessians makes careless re-expansion particularly vulnerable too. spray.py:32.

3. What I would check to be sure

  • Freeze initial conditions, seed, release epochs, score settings and production AGAMA build for paired comparisons.
  • For purported exact changes, require exact retained arrays and scores. Preserve RNG draw order: initial conditions are generated before subsetting. spray.py:134.
  • For approximate changes, predeclare a systematic score-error budget substantially below 30–45—for example 5—and bound the paired mean error with uncertainty. Also inspect per-star errors, model rankings, track-bin shifts, widths and tails.
  • Establish convergence against tighter integration and denser trajectory sampling; agreement with the current baseline alone does not establish accuracy.
  • Keep optimized outputs separate from reference results, with parameter-complete cache keys and source/input hashes. Existing training resumption explicitly rejects incompatible manifests. training_set.py:155, training_set.py:239.

docs.title: Codex stepback 2026 10 10
docs.text: The premise about Ibata+2019 is already corrected in the project record: its “knee” is a sky feature near the cluster, and the record says no published model reproduces the DR3 proper motion knee at issue here. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:18–21

docs.title: 1. What has been tested
docs.text:
“Ruled out” is too strong for several entries. Some tests reject a specific implementation or parameter range; they do not eliminate the broader physical explanation.

Hypothesis What the record says; how decisive it is Code, coordinate, or sign errors Bar timing, force derivatives, centre orbit, frame round trips, arm labels, data integrity, and rotation sense were audited. The recorded checks passed, including round-trip transforms and bar-orientation checks. This is good evidence against those specific implementation errors, not a proof that every pipeline choice is correct. packet:2762–2775 docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:14–20 The measured PM knee is a STREAMFINDER selection artefact An independent Gaia selection found the PM overdensity through phi1≈24, but no independent detection beyond 26. It weakens the selection explanation over the covered range; the steepest part remains unverified independently. packet:2786–2794 The statistic creates the angle preference or knee misfit Injection tests recovered 28° truth in 100/100 mocks and 20° truth in 20/24. That supports angle recovery in this restricted setup; it does not validate the full likelihood under real model misspecification. The record itself says likelihood differences are overconfident, mock calibration is incomplete, and sensitivity to chi-bin choices remains a check. docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:21, 55–60, 104–107 packet:2807–2812 packet:3008–3012 Cluster rotation Fitted, maximal, reversed, and even 10× rotation runs did not fix the PM mismatch; the measured rotation in the escape region is small. This makes rotation an unlikely fix within those prescriptions, but does not cover every rotating progenitor structure or early history. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:61–70 packet:2754–2756 Spray release prescription A tracer comparison was reported to miss the knee at least as badly as the spray, arguing against a spray-only defect. The record notes the 28° tracer comparison was not run, so the test is incomplete. packet:2766–2767 docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:61–62 Debris age or release history Age-cut rescoring at 500, 700, and 1000 Myr left the angle ranking similar; pericentre-concentrated release worsened the fit. That does not test debris older than the available integration or release window. Thus “older debris ruled out” is broader than the evidence. packet:2776–2778 packet:2750–2753 Axisymmetric host, host mass, or halo shape DB98 and McMillan17 runs did not produce the knee; tested flattening, disc/halo changes at fixed circular speed, and host-wide mass scalings did not solve the joint fit. The mass sweep tested a finite set around Hunter+2024, not arbitrary force profiles. Reject those sampled variants, not potential-shape explanations in general. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:9–17 packet:2980–3003 Bar causes the knee A rotating Hunter+2024 bar steepened pmdec and bent the sky track partway; it did not reproduce the full bend. Bar speed, amplitude, size, and angle were then varied. The residual pmdec mismatch persists, and the angle preference is not established: one profile-stage search found the 16°/28° difference within seed noise, while earlier fixed-grid comparisons favored 16°. packet:2374–2399 packet:3014–3024 Bar model and time dependence Portail+2017, longer-bar variants, and slowing-bar variants were tested. The slowing-bar grid re-scanned today’s pattern speed over 31–34, but only for the listed eta values and with a limited parameter combination; it does not exhaust time-dependent bar histories or bar-phase uncertainty. docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:61–62 bin/streams/phase2b_grid.py:2–6, 18–21 Distance step explains the PM bend The earlier CMD analysis found no ~30% step, but its normalization was later judged unreliable and distance was dropped from the fit. Treat a large step as unsupported by that analysis, not definitively excluded; the distance-free likelihood leaves distance and transverse velocity partly degenerate. docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:66–68, 76–83 packet:2893–2897 Solar frame, omega Cen state, or distance The Ibata frame strongly improved the knee score, but its solar motion conflicts with the stated Sgr A* constraint. Frame decomposition attributed the gain mainly to the cluster’s Galactocentric initial velocity, at a cost near the cluster. PM shifts improved the score toward the edge of the tested ±2σ grid; the profile stage later allowed ±3σ but was sparse. These are important degeneracies, not settled physical fixes. packet:2913–2922 packet:2948–2966 packet:3014–3024 Omega Cen mass or dark matter Changing cluster mass by factors 0.7 and 1.5 did not move the PM medians into agreement; the larger mass worsened the score. This tests those mass scalings, not self-gravity of old debris. packet:3026–3031 Sagittarius perturbation The recorded integrations put Sgr at least about 10 kpc from the stream during the tested 600 Myr and estimate a far-too-small differential kick. Strong evidence against Sgr as the recent cause under those assumptions. packet:2350–2357 LMC and reflex motion Not implemented in the stream model, so untested. The early literature estimate that it was secondary is not a simulation result. docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:48–49 Different progenitor, shared debris, or knee not from recent omega Cen debris Chemistry is suggestive but based on small bright-star samples; the record calls broader XP results inconclusive. Stream 55’s relation and the knee’s ancestry remain open. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:28–31 packet:2319–2333 Self-gravity of old debris The cited Ibata+2019 model used live N-body and says earlier debris gravity mattered, but the present project deliberately excludes live N-body. This explanation is outside the allowed model, not ruled out by these tests. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:121–124, 134–138

Tests repeated or overlapping: DB98 was used both for debris morphology and for the observed-star backtrack; those address different questions, so the second is not a redundant rerun. Rotation was probed through several related setups (fitted, maximal, and exaggerated), making the repeated negative result more useful but still limited to those implementations. Bar speed and bar size were scanned in successive grids, with some overlap. The larger issue is not literal repetition: “older debris ruled out,” “selection ruled out,” and “the angle is preferred” each overstate what the recorded tests establish. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:98–102 packet:2374–2399 packet:3014–3024

docs.title: 2. Is the explanation space exhausted?
docs.text:
No. A useful first gate is still missing: the existing backtrack compares observed stars with omega Cen’s orbit in static McMillan17 and DB98 hosts, over distances 2.5–6.5 kpc and 1.5 Gyr. Its scalar metric is a fixed weighted distance in position and velocity; it does not propagate measurement or cluster-state uncertainty. bin/streams/backtrack_fimbulthul.py:15–16, 34–47

The rotating-bar machinery exists, including bar speed, present angle, slowing rate, amplitude, and size. That makes the proposed barred backtrack feasible, but the current star-backtrack script does not use it. src/ocen_dm/streams/restricted.py:40–58, 60–89

Still genuinely open are:

  • Whether knee stars can reach a recent release region in a plausible barred potential once astrometric, RV, distance, and omega Cen state uncertainties are propagated. The current backtrack uses point estimates for the listed observables and a distance grid, and fixes the cluster phase-space point. bin/streams/backtrack_fimbulthul.py:26–47
  • Debris older than the tested window, alternative progenitor structure or ancestry, and live self-gravity (the last is excluded by the PI’s constraint). docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:47–49 docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:121–124, 134–138
  • LMC reflex, broader time-dependent bar histories, and potential families beyond the sampled variants. docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:45–49
  • The interpretation of the PM ridge beyond phi1≈24, where the independent selection did not recover a clear detection. packet:2789–2794

docs.title: 3. Is the barred-backtrack “kill test” right?
docs.text:
Yes, as a gate before further tuning, but it needs a better target than “closest to the cluster’s orbit.” The existing test compares star and cluster trajectories using \(dx/0.2\) kpc and \(dv/20\) km/s, then takes the minimum over time and scanned distance. That is a useful diagnostic, but the scales are chosen constants, not propagated uncertainties or a release model. bin/streams/backtrack_fimbulthul.py:2–5, 43–47

For the bar run, sample each star’s position, PMs, parallax or distance constraint, and RV uncertainty; sample omega Cen’s present state and the allowed host/bar parameters with their relevant constraints. Integrate both trajectories in the same time-dependent potential, with the present bar phase tied to its allowed angle range. Then measure whether the star’s uncertainty region intersects the modeled escape/release distribution—including finite tidal radius and escape velocity—not whether the star and cluster must occupy identical phase space. The bar implementation supports time-dependent rotation and slowing histories. src/ocen_dm/streams/restricted.py:40–58, 60–89

I would abandon recent omega Cen debris in the tested barred, test-particle framework if the knee-star posterior repeatedly misses every plausible recent release distribution over the model’s relevant release ages, while the same method recovers the near-cluster arm and injected mock debris. That would reject the framework’s recent-release explanation; it would not prove that the stars never came from omega Cen, since older debris, self-gravity, or a different history remain outside that test.

docs.title: 4. Ranked plan
docs.text:
1. Run the barred reachability test first. Predefine the allowed bar and cluster-state ranges, release-age range, and overlap statistic; calibrate the threshold on near-cluster members and mock releases. Stop tuning if the knee stars remain incompatible across those ranges and mocks pass. Continue if a substantial knee subset overlaps plausible release regions.

  2. Resolve the observational edge and ancestry only if step 1 passes or is ambiguous. Extend an independent Gaia/RV/chemistry check through the distal knee; the current independent PM detection stops short of its steepest part. Go if the same coherent PM track and compatible velocities persist; otherwise describe the distal feature’s membership as unresolved. packet:2789–2794

  3. Only then profile the allowed barred model jointly, with multiple seeds and mocks, including the remaining plausible host, bar-history, and omega Cen state variations. Stop if no fit reproduces the knee within the stated angle/state constraints; write up a negative result: the tested recent test-particle framework can make a partial bend but cannot match the observed PM track. The record already reports the persistent pmdec residual and cautions that the fit ranking is noisy or overconfident. docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:10–21, 63–69

docs.title: What I verified, what I assume, and the counterargument
docs.text:
Verified: The static backtrack’s time window, distance scan, hosts, and metric are explicit in code. bin/streams/backtrack_fimbulthul.py:15–16, 34–47 The dated record reports the knee stars’ static-host velocity misses and documents the bar, age, selection, host-mass, and frame experiments cited above. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:98–102 docs/STREAM_DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md:55–69 packet:2780–2806

Assumptions: I take the recorded numerical results and run summaries as accurate; I did not recompute the integrations or inspect every run artifact. “Plausible barred host” needs explicit parameter bounds agreed with the project’s priors.

Strongest argument against my recommendation: A successful orbit-connection test is not required to be a close pointwise match to the cluster orbit: real escapers leave with offsets, and the record itself notes that Ibata’s explanation invokes self-gravity of earlier debris. Conversely, a failed test can falsely reject ancestry if the distance/RV posterior, old release ages, or allowed bar history is too restrictive. The proposed test is therefore decisive only for the specified recent test-particle model, not for omega Cen ancestry in general. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:121–124

To be sure: I would check the exact input uncertainties and membership of the 15 knee stars with RVs, define the bar-angle/pattern-speed prior and release distribution before seeing results, verify the time-dependent orbit integrator against mock releases, and extend the independent PM/RV check beyond phi1≈24. bin/streams/backtrack_fimbulthul.py:28–40 packet:2789–2794

docs.title: Codex review: stream paper plan (2026-10-16)
docs.text:
Question: critical review of the proposed MNRAS storyline (data, model, no fit without a bar, bar constraints) and figure plan. Ordinary Codex, effort high, read-only.

The repository contradicts two premises in the proposed storyline. The angle refinements are not converged profile fits, and 34–35 km/s/kpc is not a general constraint once bar size and angle vary: the saved sweep’s best sampled 28-degree model uses 36, and its best sampled 36-degree model uses 37. docs/STREAM_PM_REFINEMENT_2026-10-13.md:107, results/plot_data/bar3d_sweep/w0.jsonl:50, results/plot_data/bar3d_sweep/w4.jsonl:102

I would reject “impossible without a bar” as the paper’s claim. The defensible paper is a comparison: tested axisymmetric models miss the observed bend and PM gradients; barred models offer an explanation worth testing, but parameter inference remains conditional on unresolved model and selection errors. The existing axisymmetric failures are documented, while the later barred candidates retain PM residuals and external-measurement tension. docs/STREAM_KNEE_INVESTIGATION.md:9, docs/STREAM_PM_REFINEMENT_2026-10-13.md:119, docs/STREAM_PM_REFINEMENT_2026-10-13.md:128

Claims and reasoning that need correction

  • “Independent detection” needs qualification. The Gaia check avoids orbit templates, but derives its query footprint, CMD locus, and on-stream centre from STREAMFINDER members. It also includes those members in the Gaia sample. Its reported significance is the maximum over a searched PM map, without a trial correction in this script. Call it an alternative selection check, and repeat it excluding catalogue members with control-field calibration. bin/streams/m5_independent_selection.py:38, bin/streams/m5_independent_selection.py:51, bin/streams/m5_independent_selection.py:62

  • The mocks establish limited recovery, not absence of angle bias. They use two truths from the same spray family, add the scorer’s kernel widths, omit contaminants, fix candidate distance, and search only four angles. They do not calibrate false bar detections, continuous confidence intervals, or recovery under model misspecification. bin/streams/d2_mock_recovery.py:3, bin/streams/d2_mock_recovery.py:19, bin/streams/d2_mock_recovery.py:32

  • “Density-free” overstates the implemented score. The foreground conditional cancels its along-stream marginal, but foreground/background odds still depend on that marginal. Also, 5% is the joint mixture coefficient, not a fixed conditional contamination fraction. The density audit preserves the low-angle ranking for the tested candidates; it does not validate the background distribution. src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:239, src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:278, docs/STREAM_PM_REFINEMENT_2026-10-13.md:152

  • Keep score definitions separate. The older score adds sky, PM, and RV log terms; the adopted score evaluates their joint conditional mixture. The quoted distance-sensitivity experiment uses the older robust chi-KDE. Neither its numerical changes nor an older sky/PM decomposition should be presented as measurements under the final objective. Separate marginal diagnostic scores also do not add up to the joint score. src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:67, src/ocen_dm/streams/score.py:276, bin/streams/ocen_state_sensitivity.py:36, bin/streams/obs_split.py:27

The minimum fair axisymmetric test
